item.reason: The thread has one identifiable cause: an outdated dockerfile-maven-plugin version. The accepted answer's fix (upgrade to 1.4.7) is confirmed by the asker, and the error messages give enough evidence to diagnose it.
item.scenario:
Our four-person team builds a Spring Boot service into a Docker image with `mvn clean package dockerfile:build`. The build works on my colleagues' machines but fails on mine (macOS Mojave, Maven 3.5.4, Docker 18.06.1-ce build e68fc7a).

The error:

```
[ERROR] Failed to execute goal com.spotify:dockerfile-maven-plugin:1.3.6:build (default) on project spring-boot-service: Could not build image: com.spotify.docker.client.shaded.com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonMappingException: Can not construct instance of com.spotify.docker.client.messages.RegistryAuth: no String-argument constructor/factory method to deserialize from String value ('swarm')
[ERROR] at [Source: N/A; line: -1, column: -1] (through reference chain: java.util.LinkedHashMap["stackOrchestrator"])
```

An earlier run gave the same exception, but with the value ('osxkeychain').

The plugin is declared with only `<version>1.3.6</version>` and `<repository>${project.artifactId}</repository>`.

What I have tried:
- Splitting the build: `mvn package` succeeds, but the docker build goal fails with the same error.
- Wiping ~/.m2/repository.
- Restarting Docker.
- Removing all images.
- Rebooting the machine.

None of these helped.
item.root_cause: The project uses an old dockerfile-maven-plugin version (1.3.6). Its bundled docker-client cannot parse the newer Docker for Mac client config. It tries to deserialize entries such as credsStore 'osxkeychain' and stackOrchestrator 'swarm' as RegistryAuth objects and fails.
item.fix: Upgrade the plugin in the pom to the latest release, 1.4.7. Optionally bind the build/push goals in an execution and set tag and JAR_FILE buildArgs, so that `mvn clean package` builds the image. Make sure the image tag referenced in docker-compose matches the built tag (e.g. artifactId:version).
key_points: The failure comes from dockerfile-maven-plugin 1.3.6 being outdated.
The JsonMappingException arises while parsing the local Docker config entries ('osxkeychain', 'stackOrchestrator': 'swarm') as RegistryAuth.
It works for colleagues because their environment or Docker config differs; Maven cache and Docker restarts are irrelevant.
The fix is upgrading the plugin to 1.4.7.

audit.notes: The accepted answer directs upgrading dockerfile-maven-plugin to 1.4.7 and provides the updated configuration; the scenario includes the relevant error and plugin version without explicitly saying the version is wrong. An experienced engineer could infer the old plugin/version incompatibility from the Docker config deserialization error. The reference identifies one primary cause.

item.reason: The accepted answer names a clear cause for the failing name lookups: the VPN client never received the cluster DNS search domains. The scenario can include the evidence needed to infer this, namely that IP access works and bare-name lookups work inside pods, without stating the cause.
item.scenario:
We run a kylemanna/openvpn container inside our local Kubernetes cluster so developers can reach Services from their laptops. The pod network is 10.2.0.0/16 and the service network is 10.3.0.0/16. Cluster DNS is at 10.3.0.10.

The server config was generated like this:

ovpn_genconfig -u udp://192.168.10.152:1194 -n 10.3.0.10 -n 192.168.10.1 -n 8.8.8.8 -s 10.8.0.0/24 -d -p "route 10.2.0.0 255.255.0.0" -p "route 10.3.0.0 255.255.0.0"

Clients connect fine. From a connected laptop we can:
- ping pod IPs
- ping service IPs, including 10.3.0.10
- curl a Service by its IP and get correct data

Name resolution fails, though:

$ nslookup kubernetes
;; Got recursion not available from 10.3.0.10, trying next server
;; Got SERVFAIL reply from 10.3.0.10, trying next server

The same `nslookup kubernetes` (or any Service name) succeeds from inside ordinary pods, but not from inside the openvpn pod. Ping from those pods fails, and traceroute stops at the flannel hop 10.0.2.2, so we suspected ICMP or DNS was being blocked at the overlay. That has not explained the SERVFAIL.
item.root_cause: The VPN clients are not given the Kubernetes DNS search domains (cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, default.svc.cluster.local). A bare name like "kubernetes" is therefore sent to kube-dns unqualified and is not resolved as a cluster Service. Pods resolve it only because their resolv.conf already contains those search domains.
item.fix: Regenerate the OpenVPN config to push the search domains to clients, using -p "dhcp-option DOMAIN-SEARCH cluster.local" plus the svc.cluster.local and default.svc.cluster.local entries. Also replace -d with -N so NAT is enabled, which the answer found critical on Kubernetes. Resolution via curl may take a few seconds to start working after reconnecting.
key_points: DNS server reachability is fine; IP-level routing to the pod and service networks works
Short Service names need the cluster search domains (cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, default.svc.cluster.local)
Pods resolve the names because their resolv.conf has those search domains; VPN clients do not
Push DOMAIN-SEARCH dhcp-options to clients via OpenVPN, and enable NAT (-N instead of -d)

audit.notes: The accepted answer directly identifies pushing Kubernetes DNS search domains as the key for nslookup/name resolution, and also says enabling NAT with -N was critical, so the item's fix is faithful. The scenario includes enough evidence to infer missing search domains without explicitly naming them. However, the accepted answer does not describe only one cause: it emphasizes both DNS search domains for resolution and NAT as critical for the Kubernetes OpenVPN setup/curl behavior.

item.reason: Clear discovery misconfiguration: the second (non-master) node has no way to locate the master, and the accepted answer fixes it by configuring unicast discovery pointing at the master.
item.scenario:
We run a single Elasticsearch 1.x server (with Kibana) and tried to add a second server so it would join the same cluster and hold replica copies of the data. Both machines share cluster.name: elasticsearch and bind to network.host: 0.0.0.0 on http.port 9200. The first server has node.master: true. The second has node.master: false, node.data: true, index.number_of_shards: 5 and index.number_of_replicas: 1. Both use path.data /local00/elasticsearch/, path.work /local00/el_temp/ and script.disable_dynamic: true. Neither config sets node.name, and there are no discovery settings.

After we start the second node it never joins the cluster. Its log keeps repeating:

[DEBUG][action.admin.indices.get ] [Match] no known master node, scheduling a retry

The first node runs normally on its own. Requests to the second node never complete because it has no master. We suspect something is missing from the config, but we can't tell what.
item.root_cause: The second node cannot discover the master. No discovery hosts are configured, so the default multicast discovery does not find the master node. The data-only node therefore never learns of an eligible master and keeps retrying.
item.fix: On both nodes, disable multicast discovery (discovery.zen.ping.multicast.enabled: false). Set discovery.zen.ping.unicast.hosts to the master's hostname, for example ["node1.example.com"]. Give each node a unique node.name, keep the same cluster.name on both, and restart.
key_points: The non-master node has no master-eligible node it can discover, so it logs 'no known master node'.
No discovery configuration is present; the nodes rely on the default multicast discovery, which isn't finding the master.
The fix is to configure unicast discovery with discovery.zen.ping.unicast.hosts pointing at the master node and to disable multicast.
Both nodes must share the same cluster.name, and each should have a distinct node.name.

audit.notes: The accepted answer's working config directly implies the missing/incorrect discovery configuration and unicast hosts fix. The scenario is solvable because it preserves the key ES 1.x config and log evidence. However, the scenario explicitly calls out that there are no discovery settings, which strongly hints at the root cause. The item presents one primary cause: the second node cannot discover the master.

item.reason: Single identifiable cause: an AlterField that turns a boolean column into a ForeignKey, which PostgreSQL cannot cast automatically. The answer gives a concrete fix.
item.scenario:
We are moving a Django 1.8 project from SQLite to PostgreSQL. It has used built-in Django migrations (not South) from the start. Running `migrate` against a fresh Postgres database works for every app except `processes`. There, 0001_initial and 0002_auto_20150508_2149 apply, but 0003_auto_20150511_1543 fails. Postgres reports that the column cannot be cast to type integer. The same migration chain ran cleanly on SQLite.

In 0001_initial, the `Process` model is created with `milestone = models.BooleanField(default=False)` alongside name, sequence and sla. 0002 creates a new `Milestone` model with a FK to `Workflow`. It also changes Process ordering and unique_together to reference `milestone`, and removes `Process.workflow`. The failing 0003 migration contains an `AlterField` on `process.milestone` that sets it to `models.ForeignKey(to='processes.Milestone')`, plus an `AlterModelOptions` setting `verbose_name_plural`. Later migrations (0004-0008) are still unapplied. What is going wrong, and how should we fix it?
item.root_cause: Migration 0003 alters `Process.milestone` in place from a BooleanField to a ForeignKey (an integer column). PostgreSQL will not change a column's type without a cast rule for the existing data. Boolean values cannot be cast to integer FK ids, so the ALTER fails. SQLite never enforced this, so it did not complain.
item.fix: If no data needs to carry over, rewrite 0003 so it does not alter the field in place. Use `RemoveField` for `process.milestone`, then `AddField` to add `milestone` as `ForeignKey(to='processes.Milestone')`, keeping the `AlterModelOptions` operation.
key_points: The failing operation is the AlterField changing Process.milestone from BooleanField to ForeignKey
PostgreSQL requires an explicit cast/USING rule to change a column's type and cannot cast boolean to an integer FK
SQLite allowed the change, which is why the migration only fails on Postgres
Fix: drop and re-add the field (RemoveField + AddField) instead of AlterField

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: 0003 changes Process.milestone from BooleanField to ForeignKey/integer and should be rewritten as remove/add if no data migration is needed. However, the scenario explicitly describes the BooleanField, the failing AlterField to ForeignKey, and the integer cast error, which strongly hints at the root cause, so no_leak is false. The scenario is solvable and the accepted answer identifies one primary cause.

item.reason: There is one identifiable cause, Docker Hub pull throttling of CodeBuild image pulls, and a concrete remedy: pull from ECR or ECR Public instead.
item.scenario:
Our CI pipeline builds a Python application container in AWS CodeBuild. The source, including the Dockerfile, lives in CodeCommit. The Dockerfile's FROM line references a public base image by its short name, which resolves to Docker Hub. The buildspec runs a plain `docker build` with no registry login step.

Some builds have started failing during the base image pull with:

```
toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit. You may increase the limit by authenticating and upgrading: https://www.docker.com/increase-rate-limit
```

The failures are intermittent. The same commit sometimes builds fine and sometimes fails at this step. Nobody on the team pulls this image heavily from this account. We can't see why our builds would exceed any limit. Building the same image locally works.
item.root_cause: The CodeBuild job pulls its base image from Docker Hub. Docker Hub throttles image pulls, especially unauthenticated ones, so the builds hit Docker Hub's pull rate limit and the pull is rejected with toomanyrequests.
item.fix: Stop pulling base images from Docker Hub in CodeBuild. Host private images in Amazon ECR and reference public images from the Amazon ECR Public Gallery, then update the Dockerfile FROM lines to match.
key_points: The error comes from Docker Hub's pull rate limiting/throttling, not from CodeBuild or the Dockerfile itself.
The base image in FROM is being pulled from Docker Hub (unauthenticated) during the build.
Remedy is to source images from Amazon ECR (private) or the ECR Public Gallery instead of Docker Hub.

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: CodeBuild is pulling from Docker Hub and hitting Docker Hub pull throttling, with ECR/ECR Public as the recommended alternative. However, the scenario effectively gives away the cause by saying the FROM short name resolves to Docker Hub, there is no registry login, and showing the Docker Hub pull-rate-limit error.

item.reason: Clear single root cause: Data Protection keys are not shared across instances, so each container encrypts the auth cookie with its own keys.
item.scenario:
We run an ASP.NET Core 2.1 web app on Kubernetes. It signs users in with OpenID Connect against Auth0 (code flow, callback path /signin-auth0), and cookie auth is the default authenticate, sign-in and challenge scheme. SaveTokens is on, and an OnRedirectToIdentityProvider handler rewrites the redirect URI to https.

With one replica everything works. [Authorize] endpoints send anonymous users to Auth0, they log in, and they come back authenticated.

After scaling the deployment to two or more pods, logins became unreliable. Whether the callback succeeds or fails seems to depend on which pod handles it. Even after a successful login, refreshing the page repeatedly eventually lands on a pod that treats the user as anonymous and redirects them back to Auth0.

We expected cookie auth to be stateless: the browser sends the cookie, and any instance should be able to read it and recover the claims. Hours of debugging the authentication configuration in Startup.cs have not turned up anything.
item.root_cause: ASP.NET Core Data Protection encrypts the authentication cookie, and by default its key ring and isolation are scoped to each app instance. Each pod has its own keys, so a pod cannot decrypt a cookie (or correlation/state cookie) issued by another pod.
item.fix: Configure Data Protection on every instance to persist keys to a common shared location (for example a shared file system) and set the same application name. Example: services.AddDataProtection().PersistKeysToFileSystem(...).SetApplicationName("MyApp").
key_points: The auth cookie is encrypted with ASP.NET Core Data Protection.
Data Protection keys are per-instance by default, so other pods cannot decrypt the cookie.
Keys must be persisted to a shared location accessible to all instances.
All instances must use the same application name (SetApplicationName).

audit.notes: The item accurately reflects the accepted answer: ASP.NET Core Data Protection keys are instance-local by default, so cookies protected by one pod cannot be read by another; the fix is shared key persistence plus a common application name. The scenario includes the key symptoms without naming Data Protection or shared keys. It is solvable from the multi-pod cookie-auth behavior, and the reference identifies one primary cause.

item.reason: The accepted answer explains the throughput gap: the test is a single-threaded loop of synchronous round-trips, while redis-benchmark uses 50 parallel clients and may pipeline. It shows how to parallelize or pipeline to get comparable numbers.
item.scenario:
We're adding a Redis cache layer to a .NET web app using the StackExchange.Redis client. The app and Redis run on the same Windows dev machine. Running `redis-benchmark -n 100000` against the server looks great: SET about 112k req/s and GET about 124k req/s, with 99.7%+ under 1 ms. The tool reports '50 parallel clients, 3 bytes payload, keep alive: 1'.

Our xUnit perf test is much slower. It creates our CacheManager, then runs a `for` loop of 300,000 iterations. Each iteration calls `cm.SaveCache("testtesttest"+i, "t")` and then `cm.ObtainItemFromCacheString("testtesttest"+i)`. Those wrap `IDatabase.StringSet` and `IDatabase.StringGet`. The connection is a static `Lazy<ConnectionMultiplexer>` built from "localhost:6379,allowAdmin=true,abortConnect=false,ssl=false" with SyncTimeout=60000. Non-string values go through Newtonsoft.Json serialization. The test takes about 21 seconds, roughly 28k ops/s. That's far below the benchmark and close to unusable for us. Why is the client so much slower than the benchmark numbers?
item.root_cause: The test is not like-for-like with redis-benchmark. It issues one synchronous request at a time on a single thread and waits for each reply, so it is bound by round-trip latency. redis-benchmark uses 50 parallel clients, possibly pipelined, with a fixed 3-byte payload. The test's serialization and wrapper overhead add further cost.
item.fix: Benchmark only the Redis operations, using a fixed small payload with no serialization. Run the calls in parallel across many threads sharing the one ConnectionMultiplexer. Alternatively, pipeline them: use the *Async APIs or fire-and-forget flags and await only the last task. Also make sure server persistence is disabled for the benchmark.
key_points: The test loop is single-threaded and synchronous, so each operation pays a full round-trip before the next starts.
redis-benchmark uses 50 parallel clients, and possibly pipelining, so the throughput numbers are not comparable.
SE.Redis supports many threads on one multiplexer, and pipelining via *Async calls or fire-and-forget, to reach high throughput.
Serialization and wrapper overhead should be removed to benchmark one thing with a payload like the benchmark's 3 bytes.

audit.notes: The item accurately reflects the accepted answer: the benchmark comparison is not like-for-like due to synchronous per-operation usage, lack of 50-way parallelism/pipelining, payload differences, and possible extra overhead; the proposed fixes match the answer. The scenario includes the relevant benchmark details and test structure but does not explicitly state the diagnosis. An experienced engineer could infer the issue. The root cause is framed as one primary benchmarking mismatch with contributing facets, not unrelated alternative causes.

item.reason: The accepted answer names a single cause: Chrome's sandbox cannot start inside the container. It gives a concrete fix, and the scenario can carry the evidence without revealing the cause.
item.scenario:
Our Selenium integration suite runs on a Linux test host. The tests execute inside a Docker container, and the suite iterates over the browsers listed in a properties file (firefox, chrome, phantomjs). For each one it instantiates FirefoxDriver, ChromeDriver or PhantomJSDriver with default options, then runs Play's testServer with a login-and-assert callback.

The Firefox run launches and passes. The Chrome run fails every time. Output:

Starting ChromeDriver (v2.8.240825) on port 21549
PAC support disabled because there is no system implementation
Test IntegrationTest.AdminUserelementscheck failed: org.openqa.selenium.WebDriverException: chrome not reachable
(Driver info: chromedriver=2.8.240825,platform=Linux 2.6.32-431.el6.x86_64 x86_64) (WARNING: The server did not provide any stacktrace information)
Command duration or timeout: 20.83 seconds

ChromeDriver itself starts and binds its port, but the browser never becomes reachable. ChromeDriver is created with no extra ChromeOptions. Why does Chrome fail here when Firefox works in the same environment?
item.root_cause: Chrome's sandbox relies on Linux container/namespace isolation. That cannot be set up inside an unprivileged Docker container, so the Chrome process fails to start and ChromeDriver reports 'chrome not reachable'.
item.fix: Either run the Docker container with --privileged, or launch Chrome with the --no-sandbox argument (e.g., via ChromeOptions).
key_points: Chrome uses its own Linux container/namespace sandbox to run
The sandbox cannot initialize inside an unprivileged Docker container, so Chrome never starts
Fix: run the container with docker run --privileged, or start Chrome with --no-sandbox

audit.notes: The root cause and fixes match the accepted answer: Chrome cannot run normally in Docker due to its sandbox/container requirements, and the suggested fixes are --privileged or --no-sandbox. The scenario includes Docker and missing ChromeOptions as necessary evidence but does not explicitly reveal the sandbox/privilege cause. It is reasonably solvable and the reference has one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear single root cause: xdebug.remote_host set to 127.0.0.1 inside the container, so Xdebug tries to reach the container itself rather than the host running PhpStorm.
item.scenario:
I'm running a LAMP-style PHP 5.4 container under boot2docker on a Mac. The app is reachable in the browser at http://192.168.99.100:32775. It was started with:

 docker run --name lampf -d -p 32775:80 -v /Users/sja/Sites/lamkepf2:/var/www/html --link=lampf_db:db codinglimo/apache_php540_gs_imgmck_pdflib9

The bind mount works, and file edits show up immediately. I installed Xdebug in the container with this xdebug.ini:

 zend_extension="/usr/local/lib/php/extensions/no-debug-non-zts-20100525/xdebug.so"
 xdebug.remote_enable=on
 xdebug.remote_host=127.0.0.1
 xdebug.remote_port=9000
 xdebug.remote_handler=dbgp
 xdebug.profiler_enable=0
 xdebug.profiler_output_dir="/temp/profiledir"

The extension loads. PhpStorm on the Mac is listening for debug connections on port 9000, and a server/path mapping is configured for /var/www/html. Even so, when I load index.php in the browser, every breakpoint is ignored. No debug session ever appears in the IDE, and the page renders normally. What's wrong?
item.root_cause: xdebug.remote_host is set to 127.0.0.1. Inside the container that address is the container's own loopback, not the host machine running PhpStorm. Xdebug therefore never reaches the IDE listening on port 9000.
item.fix: Point xdebug.remote_host at the host's IP as seen from inside the container (by default the Docker bridge gateway, e.g. 172.17.42.1) and set xdebug.remote_connect_back=Off. Determine the host's actual IP from within the container rather than assuming the default.
key_points: 127.0.0.1 inside a container refers to the container itself, not the host or IDE
Xdebug must connect to the host machine's IP reachable from the container (e.g. the docker bridge gateway 172.17.42.1)
The default bridge IP may vary, so the actual host IP should be verified
remote_connect_back is not the recommended approach here; use an explicit remote_host

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: 127.0.0.1 inside the container is not the PhpStorm host, and xdebug.remote_host should be set to the host IP visible from the container with remote_connect_back off. The scenario includes the relevant xdebug config and Docker/boot2docker context without explicitly explaining the loopback issue. It is solvable and the accepted answer identifies one primary cause.

item.reason: The accepted answer identifies one root cause: macOS High Sierra's fork-safety change breaks Python processes that fork, which is how the scheduler launches tasks. The scenario can carry the needed evidence: a macOS host, SIGABRT (-6) only under the scheduler, and success under 'airflow test'.
item.scenario:
On my Mac laptop I run a local Airflow setup. Logs live under /Users/<me>/.../airflow/logs/. One DAG, 'stream_from_twitter', has a single PythonOperator task scheduled @hourly with retries=0. The task uses tweepy to open a filtered Twitter stream (track=['life'], languages=['en']). It reads 100 non-retweet statuses and publishes each one to a Kafka topic through a small producer wrapper.

If I run the task by hand with `airflow test stream_from_twitter stream_from_twitter_to_kafka 2020-01-20`, it works: tweets print and land in Kafka. When the scheduler picks the task up, it fails every time. The task log shows the normal DEBUG dependency checks ('Previous Dagrun State' PASSED, 'Trigger Rule' PASSED, 'Dependencies all met...'). Shortly after the task starts, the runner reports that the task exited with return code -6. No Python traceback appears from my callable. item.scenario:

item.reason: The accepted answer identifies a specific cause: in Release builds the shared field initializer `_TDBOpener` never runs, so the base constructor that creates the connection is never called. It also gives a concrete fix.
item.scenario:
We have a small VB.NET data-access layer on .NET Framework 4.6, built with VS 2017, using Npgsql 3.2.2.0 against PostgreSQL.

- `TDBACore` is an abstract base class. It holds `Friend Shared FConnection As IDbConnection` and a ref count. Its constructor calls the abstract `CreateConnection()` (which returns `New NpgsqlConnection()`) when the ref count is 0.
- `TDBOpener` is a sealed subclass with `Public Shared ReadOnly _TDBOpener As New TDBOpener()`.
- `TDBOpener` exposes `Public Shared Sub Open(cs)`, which just calls `TDBACore.OpenConnection(cs)`. That method checks `FConnection.State`, sets `ConnectionString`, and calls `Open()`.

The app calls:
`TDBOpener.Open("Server=192.168.1.10;Port=5434;UserId=postgres;Password=123456;Database=testdb;CommandTimeout=300;")`

On Windows 10 64-bit:
- **Debug build:** breakpoints show `TDBACore.New()` is hit and the connection opens fine.
- **Release build:** the constructor is never entered, the connection object is never set up, and connecting fails.

The same Release build works on a Windows 7 machine. No code differs between configurations.
item.root_cause: In Release on Win10 x64, the shared ReadOnly field `_TDBOpener` (the `New TDBOpener()` initializer) is never initialized. `TDBOpener.Open` only touches `TDBACore`'s shared members, so the subclass's static initialization is never triggered. As a result, the base constructor that assigns `FConnection` never runs and `FConnection` stays Nothing.
item.fix: Force the singleton to be created before using the connection. In `TDBOpener.Open`, add `If TDBACore.FConnection Is Nothing Then Dim obOpen = _TDBOpener` before calling `TDBACore.OpenConnection(ConnectionString)`.
key_points: The shared `_TDBOpener = New TDBOpener()` initializer does not run in the Release build.
Because the constructor never runs, `CreateConnection` is never called and the shared `FConnection` remains Nothing.
`Open` only accesses base-class shared members, so nothing forces initialization of `TDBOpener`'s static field.
Fix: explicitly reference `_TDBOpener` (e.g., when `FConnection` is Nothing) before opening.

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: the shared _TDBOpener instance is not initialized in Release, and the fix is to force access to _TDBOpener when FConnection is Nothing. item.reason: Clear diagnosis: the database's C locale (LC_CTYPE/LC_COLLATE) prevents lowercasing of Cyrillic in text search dictionaries.
item.scenario:
We're setting up full text search for Russian content in PostgreSQL. Uppercase Cyrillic words are not being normalized. For example:

SELECT * FROM to_tsvector('test_russian', 'На рынке появились новые рублевые облигации');
-> 'На':1 'новые':4 'облигации':6 'появились':3 'рублевые':5 'рынке':2

'На' is a Russian stopword and should be dropped, but it comes back unchanged and still capitalized. If the same sentence is passed already in lowercase, the stopword is removed correctly.

The custom config is a copy of 'russian'. Its word mapping goes to a simple-template dictionary (STOPWORDS = russian) followed by a snowball russian dictionary. The built-in 'russian' configuration gives exactly the same result. The docs say the simple template lowercases tokens before checking stopwords.

ts_debug shows the tokens are classified as 'word', as expected. Pre-lowercasing input in the application would work, but we'd like to understand why the dictionaries aren't lowercasing.
item.root_cause: The cluster/database was initialized with the default "C" LC_CTYPE and LC_COLLATE. Under that locale PostgreSQL's lowercasing does not handle Cyrillic characters, so dictionaries cannot fold 'На' to 'на' and the stopword match fails.
item.fix: Re-initialize the cluster with initdb using a UTF-8 locale and UTF-8 encoding. Then recreate the database with ENCODING 'UTF8', LC_COLLATE = 'ru_RU.UTF-8' and LC_CTYPE = 'ru_RU.UTF-8'. After that the simple dictionary lowercases Russian words and removes the stopwords.
key_points: Database uses C (default) LC_CTYPE/LC_COLLATE
Case folding in text search depends on LC_CTYPE, so non-ASCII Cyrillic isn't lowercased under C
Recreate cluster/database with UTF8 encoding and a ru_RU.UTF-8 (UTF-8) ctype/collate

item.scenario:
Our Spring service talks to an Elasticsearch 7.2.0 cluster using RestHighLevelClient 7.2.0. The cluster has 3 master nodes at 4 GB each and 2 data nodes at 8 GB each. The client cannot reach the nodes directly. It goes through an Azure load balancer in front of the data nodes, and only port 9200 is exposed.

At around 10-30 mixed get/put requests per second, some calls fail with java.net.SocketTimeoutException. The index is small: 2 shards, 1 replica, about 27 MB total. Dynamic mapping is disabled.

We create two client beans, one for reads and one for writes. Both use:
- basic auth
- 5 IO reactor threads
- connectTimeout 10000 ms
- socketTimeout 60000 ms
- connectionRequestTimeout 0

The failing requests do not error out quickly. They hang until the 60 s socket timeout expires and then throw. Other requests on the same client succeed. Raising timeouts and splitting read and write clients did not stop the failures. Cluster size and index size do not seem to explain it.
item.root_cause: A network device between client and cluster (the load balancer or firewall) drops idle TCP connections after its session/idle timeout. The OS TCP keepalive interval (net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time, default 7200 s) is longer than that timeout, so no keepalive probe is sent before the drop. The async HTTP client keeps reusing these silently dropped pooled connections and waits until the socket timeout fires.
item.fix: Find any load balancer, firewall or proxy in the path that has an idle/session timeout. Either increase that idle timeout, or lower the client host's TCP keepalive time (net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time) so probes are sent before the device drops the connection.
key_points: An intermediate network device (load balancer or firewall) silently drops idle connections after its idle timeout
The kernel tcp_keepalive_time (default 7200 s) is longer than the device timeout, so no keepalive probe is sent in time
The Elasticsearch async HTTP client reuses dead pooled connections and hangs until the socket timeout
Fix by raising the device idle timeout or lowering the TCP keepalive interval

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: an intermediate network device idle/session timeout is shorter than OS TCP keepalive, causing silently dropped connections that only fail at socket timeout; fix is to adjust the device timeout or TCP keepalive. item.reason: The thread has a single identifiable cause. The Lambda source_code_hash never reflects the zip contents, so Terraform detects no code change. The accepted answer fixes this by deriving the hash from an archive_file data source.
item.scenario:
We deploy a Python Lambda with Terraform (0.11-style syntax, AWS provider). The repo has a lambda module with files/lambda_function.py.

On every apply, a null_resource with an always-changing uuid() trigger runs several local-exec provisioners. They remove and recreate ${path.module}/files/zips, copy the .py file in, and run `zip -r lambda.zip .`.

The aws_lambda_function resource is configured as follows:
- filename = "${path.module}/files/zips/lambda.zip"
- source_code_hash = "${base64sha256(format("%s/files/zips/lambda.zip", path.module))}"
- depends_on the null_resource

When I edit lambda_function.py and run terraform apply, it completes without errors and the zip is regenerated locally. However, the code running in AWS Lambda is still the old version. If I delete the Terraform state files and apply from scratch, the new code shows up fine. Why aren't code edits reaching the deployed function?
item.root_cause: source_code_hash is computed with base64sha256() over a formatted path string, not over the zip file's contents. The hash therefore never changes when the code changes, so Terraform sees no diff on the Lambda function and never re-uploads the package. The zip is also only built by a null_resource provisioner during apply, so nothing at plan time reflects the new contents.
item.fix: Replace the null_resource zipping with a `data "archive_file"` that builds lambda.zip from the Python file. Set source_code_hash = data.archive_file.lambda_zip.output_base64sha256 so the hash tracks the actual archive contents and triggers an update whenever the code changes.
key_points: base64sha256(format(...path...)) hashes the path string, not the file contents, so the hash is constant
An unchanged source_code_hash means Terraform detects no change and does not update the Lambda code
Use the archive_file data source to build the zip
Set source_code_hash from archive_file's output_base64sha256

item.reason: The accepted answer names one cause: with Npgsql's default minimum pool size of 0, idle pooled connections are closed, so later opens create new physical connections. It also gives a concrete fix.
item.scenario:
We run a small .NET Core 3.1 service (Npgsql 4.1.1, also tried 4.1.2) against an Azure-hosted PostgreSQL 9.6 database. It is a health-check endpoint that runs SELECT 1 on a timer. Each request creates a new NpgsqlConnection with `await using` and calls OpenAsync.

Connection string: Server=...; User Id=...; Database=...; Port=5432; Password=...; SSLMode=Prefer. Removing SSL on both the client and the server made no difference.

Timings from our log:
```
5:13:32 PM: SLOW QUERY, CONN TIME: 4153, QUERY TIME: 18
5:13:53 PM: SLOW QUERY, CONN TIME: 707, QUERY TIME: 17
5:14:14 PM: SLOW QUERY, CONN TIME: 589, QUERY TIME: 16
5:14:35 PM: SLOW QUERY, CONN TIME: 663, QUERY TIME: 18
```
The query itself is fast, but every OpenAsync takes 500-700 ms. A Node.js app on the same machine hitting the same DB takes ~640 ms on first connect, then ~22 ms per request. psping to port 5432 shows ~1 ms latency.

The behaviour is the same running locally and on Azure App Service. We assumed connection pooling would be on by default with this connection string, but it behaves as if every open makes a brand-new connection.
item.root_cause: Npgsql's pool defaults to a Min Pool Size of 0. With requests this infrequent, the pool closes the idle physical connection, so most OpenAsync calls must set up a full new connection (TCP, SSL and authentication) to Azure Postgres.
item.fix: Add a minimum pool size to the connection string, e.g. `Minimum Pool Size=1` or higher. This keeps that many physical connections open regardless of usage, so OpenAsync reuses a warm connection.
key_points: Npgsql pooling is enabled, but the default Min Pool Size is 0
Idle pooled connections get closed when the endpoint is called infrequently
Each OpenAsync then pays the full connection-setup cost, not a pool reuse
Fix: set Minimum Pool Size in the connection string to keep connections alive

item.reason: Clear network diagnosis: the host has no working route to the boot2docker host-only subnet. The answer gives a concrete fix, adding a route via the vboxnet interface.
item.scenario:
Developer workstation: MacBook running OS X 10.9.5 Mavericks. Docker was installed per the official Mac guide, with boot2docker 1.3.1 and Docker 1.3.1 running in VirtualBox. It is a corporate laptop with the standard company networking/security client installed.

`boot2docker status` reports `running`. `boot2docker ip` returns 192.168.59.103. Every docker client command from the Mac hangs and then fails:

```
docker run hello-world
Post https://192.168.59.103:2376/v1.15/containers/create: dial tcp 192.168.59.103:2376: i/o timeout
docker search ubuntu
Get https://192.168.59.103:2376/v1.15/images/search?term=ubuntu: dial tcp 192.168.59.103:2376: i/o timeout
```

Inside the VM, reached via `boot2docker ssh`, the daemon is up and listening on the expected port:

```
sudo netstat -ntpl | grep docker
tcp 0 0 :::2376 :::* LISTEN 629/docker
```

So the daemon is running and the port matches. Yet the Mac cannot reach it at the host-only IP. No error is returned, only a timeout.
item.root_cause: The Mac's routing table no longer sends traffic for 192.168.59.0/24 out the VirtualBox host-only interface (vboxnetN). Packets to the VM's IP go elsewhere and time out. This is commonly caused by VPN software such as Cisco AnyConnect taking over the routes.
item.fix: In VirtualBox, check the boot2docker VM's network settings to find the host-only adapter's name (e.g. vboxnet0 or vboxnet1). Then add a route for the subnet over that interface: `sudo route -nv add -net 192.168.59 -interface vboxnet1`.
key_points: The daemon is listening fine; the problem is host-side network routing, not Docker itself
Traffic to the 192.168.59.x host-only subnet is not being routed through the vboxnet interface
VPN client software (e.g. Cisco AnyConnect) is a common culprit for hijacking the route
Fix by manually adding a route for 192.168.59.0 via the correct vboxnetN interface

item.reason: The thread is a single diagnosable problem: the upstart docker job is broken, and the accepted answer traces it to two conflicting Docker packages being installed at once.
item.scenario:
Ubuntu 14.04 host, Docker client 1.2.0 (API 1.14, go1.3.1). Docker had been working for weeks. Following a tuning guide, I added two lines to /etc/init/docker.conf:
```
limit memlock unlimited unlimited
limit nofile 262144
```
I then ran `sudo /etc/init.d/docker restart`. It replied: "Docker is managed via upstart, try using service docker restart". So I ran `sudo service docker restart`, which printed:
```
stop: Unknown job: docker
start: Unknown job: docker
```
The daemon will not come back, even after a reboot. `sudo docker version` prints the client info and then fails with:
`dial unix /var/run/docker.sock: no such file or directory`
Running `sudo docker -d` manually in a terminal works, and other shells can use Docker normally while it runs. The service just won't start on its own.
While investigating I found two near-identical upstart files, /etc/init/docker.conf and /etc/init/docker.io.conf. `sudo service --status-all | grep docker` lists both a `docker` service and a `docker.io` service.
item.root_cause: Two different Docker packages are installed side by side. One is Ubuntu's `docker.io` package and the other is `lxc-docker` from the get.docker.io repository. Their upstart job definitions (docker.conf and docker.io.conf) conflict, so upstart no longer recognises a working `docker` job.
item.fix: Keep only one Docker package and remove the other, for example with `apt-get remove docker.io` or `apt-get remove lxc-docker`. If `sudo service docker restart` still fails afterwards, manually remove the leftover upstart and init files in /etc/ (such as the stale /etc/init/*.conf) so that a single clean job remains.
key_points: Both the Ubuntu docker.io package and the lxc-docker package (from get.docker.io) are installed
The duplicate /etc/init/docker.conf and docker.io.conf files and the two services come from these two packages
Only one Docker package should be installed; remove the other
Package removal may leave files behind, so leftover config in /etc/ may need manual cleanup

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: shell-form CMD makes /bin/sh PID 1, so gunicorn master never receives SIGTERM.
item.scenario:
We run a minimal gunicorn 19.7.1 WSGI app in a container built from the official python image, managed with docker-compose 1.12.0 (compose file v3, one service exposing 8000). Every `docker-compose stop` takes exactly 10 seconds, which matches compose's default stop timeout before it force-kills the container. Replacing the container by running `docker-compose up -d` again with a new image shows the same 10s delay. The app is trivial (a single function returning 'Hello, World!'), so it's not long-running requests.

Dockerfile:
```
FROM python
RUN pip install gunicorn
COPY test.py .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD gunicorn -b :8000 test:app
```

Gunicorn's source has signal handlers for graceful shutdown, so we expected it to exit promptly on stop. Why does the container hang until it gets killed, and how can we get a fast, graceful shutdown?
item.root_cause: The shell-form CMD runs the command via `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell is PID 1 in the container and gunicorn's master is a child process. Docker's SIGTERM goes to PID 1 (the shell), which doesn't forward it, so gunicorn never shuts down gracefully and is killed after the 10s timeout.
item.fix: Make gunicorn PID 1, e.g. `CMD exec gunicorn -b :8000 test:app` (or use exec-form JSON CMD), so it receives SIGTERM directly and shuts down gracefully.
key_points: Shell-form CMD wraps the process in /bin/sh -c, making sh PID 1
docker-compose stop sends SIGTERM to PID 1 only; the shell doesn't forward it to gunicorn
After the timeout docker sends SIGKILL, hence the consistent 10s delay
Using exec (or exec-form CMD) makes gunicorn master PID 1 so it handles SIGTERM

audit.notes: The item accurately captures the accepted answer: shell-form CMD makes /bin/sh PID 1, so gunicorn does not receive SIGTERM; using exec makes gunicorn PID 1. The scenario includes the necessary Dockerfile evidence without explicitly revealing the diagnosis. The problem is solvable from the provided details, and the accepted answer identifies one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: the Docker client needs a TLS endpoint on a dedicated port that maps to the Nexus docker repository's HTTP connector. Nginx only proxied the main Nexus port, so login either reached the Nexus UI/root and got a 404, or hit the plain HTTP connector directly.
item.scenario:
We run Nexus Repository Manager OSS 3.0.1-01 on an Ubuntu VM. Nginx sits in front of it and terminates HTTPS using a CA-signed certificate. A Maven repository behind this setup works fine from client machines. We also created a docker (hosted) repository and gave it an HTTP connector on port 4444. Using --insecure-registry on clients is not allowed.

Results of `docker login` with admin credentials:
- `docker login box.company.net` returns a Nexus HTML page titled "404 - Nexus Repository Manager".
- `docker login box.company.net:4444` fails with `Get https://box.company.net:4444/v1/users/: http: server gave HTTP response to HTTPS client`.
- After enabling an HTTPS connector on 4445 in the Nexus repo settings, `docker login box.company.net:4445` fails with `dial tcp x.x.x.x:4445: getsockopt: connection refused`.

The nginx error log is empty. The nginx access log shows only plain GETs. The Docker daemon log shows the same 404s. We are unsure whether a docker (group) repository is also required.
item.root_cause: Docker requires the registry on its own host:port over TLS, which Nexus serves only through the repository-specific connector port 4444, and that port speaks plain HTTP. Nginx was only proxying the main Nexus web port. Requests to the bare hostname therefore reached Nexus's UI and returned 404, while requests to 4444 hit plain HTTP directly.
item.fix: Add a second nginx server block that listens on a dedicated port (e.g. 6666) with SSL enabled and the CA certificate. It should proxy_pass to http://<nexus-host>:4444, the docker repository's HTTP connector, with the Host, X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto https headers, plus a large client_max_body_size and chunked transfer enabled. Restart nginx, then run `docker login`, pull and push against box.company.net:6666.
key_points: Docker registry access in Nexus 3 goes through the repository's dedicated connector port, not the main Nexus UI port/path
The Nexus docker connector on 4444 is plain HTTP, but the Docker client insists on HTTPS
Nginx must provide a separate TLS-terminating server block on a new port that proxies to the docker connector port
A group repository is not required; the missing reverse-proxy mapping was the issue
item.technology: nginx, Docker, Sonatype Nexus Repository Manager 3

audit.notes: The accepted answer directly fixes the issue by adding a separate SSL-enabled nginx server block on a dedicated port that proxies to the Nexus Docker HTTP connector on 4444, then using that nginx port for docker login/push/pull. The item's root cause is a reasonable direct implication of that fix. The scenario includes the necessary symptoms without explicitly naming the missing nginx server block, and it points to one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear single root cause: the Docker container has no init system, so Upstart service management silently does nothing. Scenario evidence (Docker, Upstart message, no output, empty logs, direct mongod works) supports diagnosis.
item.scenario:
I'm building a server image from the ubuntu:14.04 Docker base. I installed MongoDB 2.6.4 from the official apt repo, following the vendor's Ubuntu install guide. I'm working in an interactive shell inside the container.

Running `service mongod start` doesn't start anything. It just prints a notice that the script has been converted to an Upstart job and suggests `stop mongod ; start mongod`.

I tried `start mongod`. It returned with no output at all. /var/log/mongodb is completely empty, and /var/lib/mongodb (owned by mongodb:mongodb) is also empty.

The mongo shell fails with:
`warning: Failed to connect to 127.0.0.1:27017, reason: errno:111 Connection refused` ... `exception: connect failed`.

I went through common troubleshooting steps (permissions, lock files, data dirs) with no change.

The only thing that works is launching the binary by hand: `mongod --verbose &`. That starts normally with dbpath=/data/db and logs 'waiting for connections on port 27017', and after that the shell connects fine. Why won't the service start the normal way?
item.root_cause: Docker containers don't run a full init system such as Upstart. The container runs only its single command, which here is the interactive shell. So `service`/`start mongod` has no init daemon to talk to, and mongod is never launched.
item.fix: Don't rely on service/Upstart inside the container. Run /usr/bin/mongod directly as the container's command, for example via CMD/ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile, or run it in the background in an interactive session. Alternatively, use the official mongo image from Docker Hub.
key_points: Docker containers lack a full init system; Upstart/service jobs don't work inside them
The container runs a single process (here the interactive shell), so no init daemon is managing services
mongod must be launched directly (e.g. as the container CMD/ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile) or the official mongo image used

audit.notes: The item accurately reflects the accepted answer: Upstart/service management does not work normally inside a Docker container without a full init system, and the intended fix is to run mongod directly as the container command or use a proper Dockerfile/official image. The scenario includes Docker/container context as necessary evidence but does not explicitly reveal the init-system root cause. item.scenario:
Rails 4.0.0 app on PostgreSQL. A controller loops over factors and creates child records. For each factor it copies `params["factorScore_#{f.id}"]` into `params['score']`, then calls `new_scorecard.scorecard_scores.create(params.permit(:score))`. Every create fails with:

The trace points into the postgresql_adapter `exec_cache` / `exec_insert` path. Things already tried:
- Calling `.to_i` on the param.
- Hardcoding a literal integer for score.

Neither changed the error. The scorecard_scores table and its migration are new this week. The developer first wrote the migration with a different definition, ran `rake db:rollback`, edited the migration and re-ran it. The development server has been running throughout. The DB schema now shows `score` as integer.
item.root_cause: The `score` column was originally migrated as text, then rolled back and re-migrated as integer. The long-running Rails server process still held the old cached column metadata, so ActiveRecord kept typecasting and binding the value as text.

The running Rails server kept stale cached column/schema info for the table.
Casting the value in Ruby (`to_i`) doesn't help, because ActiveRecord casts it using the cached text type.
Restarting the Rails server resolves the error.

item.reason: Clear error with identifiable root cause: missing /etc/protocols because the netbase package is absent in the minimal Ubuntu image.
item.scenario:
We deploy a Yesod web app to Heroku as a Docker container. The app sends mail through Amazon SES. Under `yesod devel` on a developer laptop, email sending works. In the deployed container, every send attempt fails with an http-client exception:

```
HttpExceptionRequest Request { host = "email.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com" port = 443 secure = True ... method = "POST" ... }
 (ConnectionFailure Network.BSD.getProtocolByName: does not exist (no such protocol name: tcp))
```

The container runs the compiled binary built with `stack build`. The Dockerfile is:

```
FROM ubuntu:17.04
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y libpq-dev
WORKDIR /app
ADD . /app
EXPOSE 8080
ENV PGHOST localhost
CMD "./run"
```

The rest of the app comes up. Only the outbound SES call fails. We suspect something is missing from the image but don't know what.

The netbase package provides /etc/protocols and is absent from the minimal Ubuntu image
After fixing that, ca-certificates is needed for the HTTPS/TLS connection to SES to validate the certificate

item.reason: The accepted answer pins the timeout on one cause, thread pool starvation from a low minimum worker thread count, and the exception text in the question contains the evidence needed to reach it.
item.scenario:
Our ASP.NET Core service uses a 6-node Redis cluster (3 masters, 3 replicas) as a cache through StackExchange.Redis 2.0.601. Every so often, cache reads fail with this exception:

StackExchange.Redis.RedisTimeoutException: Timeout awaiting response (outbound=0KiB, inbound=5KiB, 5504ms elapsed, timeout is 5000ms), command=GET, next: GET CRM.UsersMainService.GetUserInfoAsync.vvs1@domain.org, inst: 0, qu: 0, qs: 6, aw: False, rs: DequeueResult, ws: Idle, in: 0, in-pipe: 5831, out-pipe: 0, serverEndpoint: 5.178.85.30:7002, mgr: 9 of 10 available, IOCP: (Busy=0,Free=1000,Min=2,Max=1000), WORKER: (Busy=10,Free=32757,Min=2,Max=32767), v: 2.0.601.3402

The cluster nodes look healthy. The failures are intermittent and line up with periods of higher traffic. The command is a simple GET on a small key. Please find out why these operations are timing out.
item.root_cause: The .NET thread pool's minimum worker thread count is set to the default of 2, which is too low for the traffic. Under load the pool has to create extra worker threads gradually (here it grew to Busy=10). The Redis response processing waits for those threads and exceeds the 5000ms timeout.
item.fix: Raise the thread pool minimum at application startup, for example ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(10, 10). Then tune the values through load testing.
key_points: The WORKER stats show Busy=10 with Min=2: busy threads exceed the minimum, so the pool is starved
The .NET thread pool injects new threads slowly once the minimum is exceeded, and the Redis operation waits during this time
Use ThreadPool.SetMinThreads at startup to raise the worker and IOCP minimums

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: low ThreadPool minimum worker threads causing delayed thread creation under load, fixed by increasing min threads with ThreadPool.SetMinThreads and tuning. The scenario includes the relevant exception diagnostics but does not explicitly name the thread pool minimum as the cause. It is solvable from the WORKER Busy/Min values and traffic context. The accepted answer identifies a single primary cause.

item.reason: The thread has one identifiable cause: pgbouncer transaction pooling breaks session-scoped prepared statements. The accepted answer fixes it by switching to session pooling with a reset query.
item.scenario:
We run a small Sinatra app under Passenger with ActiveRecord. It talks to a local PostgreSQL through pgbouncer on port 5444. The app intermittently raises:

PG::Error: ERROR: prepared statement "a2" does not exist

The failing code is a simple lookup:
  self.where("user_id=? AND key=?", id, key).first

Most requests succeed; the errors appear randomly under normal traffic. Relevant pgbouncer.ini settings:
  pool_mode=transaction
  ; server_reset_query=DISCARD ALL;   (commented out)
  server_check_delay=0
  server_check_query=SELECT 1;
  auth_type=trust

database.yml uses the postgresql adapter with host localhost, port 5444 and reconnect: true. We experimented with toggling prepared_statements in database.yml. Since then we have also seen errors like "bind message supplies 2 parameters, but prepared statement \"a1\" requires 0". Statement-level logging is now enabled in PostgreSQL. We'd like to know why the prepared statements keep going missing or mismatching, and whether disabling them entirely is the only option.
item.root_cause: pgbouncer is running with pool_mode=transaction, so successive transactions from one client can be served by different PostgreSQL backend connections. ActiveRecord's prepared statements are tied to a single backend session, so they are missing or mismatched when a later query reaches another backend. No reset query clears prepared state between clients.
item.fix: Set pool_mode=session in pgbouncer.ini and uncomment server_reset_query=DISCARD ALL so each client keeps one backend connection and prepared state is cleared when the connection is reused. Prepared_statements can then stay enabled (true) in database.yml.
key_points: Transaction pooling hands successive transactions to different server connections, but prepared statements exist only in one backend session.
Prepared statements are therefore missing or mismatched on whichever backend later receives the EXECUTE/bind.
Switching pgbouncer to session pooling keeps a client on one backend.
Enabling server_reset_query=DISCARD ALL clears leftover prepared statements before a connection is reused.

audit.notes: The item’s fix matches the accepted answer: use pgbouncer session pooling, enable server_reset_query=DISCARD ALL, and keep prepared_statements enabled. The stated explanation about transaction pooling breaking backend-session-bound prepared statements is directly implied by that fix and the original symptoms. The scenario includes the relevant config but does not explicitly reveal the diagnosis. It is solvable from the included evidence, and the reference centers on one primary cause/configuration issue rather than multiple alternatives.

`[ERROR] [FATAL] InnoDB: Table flags are 0 in the data dictionary but the flags in file ./ibdata1 are 0x4000!`

item.reason: The accepted answer gives a concrete diagnosis with a clear fix. nginx's resolver sends bare short names, and the sidecar was not expanding them with the cluster search domains. The AAAA lookups also failed.
item.scenario:
We run an nginx 1.10.0 reverse proxy in a Kubernetes pod. It should route /<name> to http://<name>:80, where <name> is an in-cluster Service. The config uses a regex location: `set $backend "http://$1:80"; proxy_pass $backend;`.

The first attempt logged `no resolver defined to resolve http://myservice`.

We then added a go-dnsmasq sidecar (janeczku/go-dnsmasq:release-1.0.5) to the same pod with args `--listen 0.0.0.0:53`. We also added `resolver 127.0.0.1:53;` to the location block.

Now `curl localhost:8080/myservice` returns 502, and nginx logs:
`myservice could not be resolved (2: Server failure), client: 127.0.0.1, server: nginx-proxy, request: "GET /myservice HTTP/1.1"`

Checks so far:
- `netstat -ntlp` in the dnsmasq container shows go-dnsmasq listening on :::53.
- nmap from the nginx container shows 53/tcp and 53/udp open on localhost.

The DNS sidecar is clearly reachable, yet the service name still fails to resolve.
item.root_cause: nginx's built-in resolver queries the bare short name (e.g. 'myservice') and does not use the pod's resolv.conf search domains. go-dnsmasq was started without --append-search-domains or --default-resolver, so it could not expand the name to the cluster FQDN and returned a server failure. nginx also issued IPv6 (AAAA) lookups, which failed.
item.fix: Start go-dnsmasq with `--listen 127.0.0.1:53 --default-resolver --append-search-domains --hostsfile=/etc/hosts` so it expands short names using the pod's search domains. Then set `resolver 127.0.0.1:53 ipv6=off;` in nginx.
key_points: nginx's resolver does not apply the resolv.conf search domains to short service names
go-dnsmasq must be run with --append-search-domains (and --default-resolver) to expand names like 'myservice' to the cluster FQDN
nginx's resolver should be set with ipv6=off to avoid the failing AAAA lookups
Port 53 being open does not mean resolution works; the failure is in name expansion, not connectivity

audit.notes: The fix exactly matches the accepted answer, and the root-cause explanation is a reasonable direct inference from adding go-dnsmasq default/search-domain flags and nginx ipv6=off. The scenario gives the same symptoms and configuration without explicitly naming search domains, default resolver, or IPv6 as the fix. An experienced engineer could plausibly diagnose it from the nginx dynamic resolver/Kubernetes DNS context. However, the reference root cause is compound: missing go-dnsmasq resolver/search-domain behavior plus nginx IPv6/AAAA lookup handling, so it is not a single primary cause.

item.scenario:
I'm setting up a Django project on Arch Linux to use PostgreSQL via psycopg2. psycopg2 was pip-installed into a Python 3.4 virtualenv (temp-python). Running `python manage.py migrate` fails before any database work happens.

The first exception in the traceback comes from Django's postgresql backend at `import psycopg2 as Database`:

```
File ".../site-packages/psycopg2/__init__.py", line 50, in <module>
  from psycopg2._psycopg import ( # noqa
ImportError: .../site-packages/psycopg2/.libs/libresolv-2-c4c53def.5.so: symbol __res_maybe_init, version GLIBC_PRIVATE not defined in file libc.so.6 with link time reference
```

A second traceback then follows during `django.setup()` → `apps.populate()` → `import_models`. It is triggered when connecting/models.py imports `django.contrib.auth.models.User` and Django tries to access the default connection.

item.root_cause: The psycopg2 package was installed from a prebuilt binary wheel, which is affected by a known psycopg2 bug. Its bundled libresolv library (.libs/libresolv-*.so) references a private glibc symbol (__res_maybe_init@GLIBC_PRIVATE) that the system's libc.so.6 doesn't provide, so the C extension fails to load.

The bundled libresolv in the psycopg2 binary wheel is incompatible with the system glibc (GLIBC_PRIVATE symbol missing)
This is a known bug in older psycopg2 binary wheels
Reinstalling with --no-binary psycopg2 avoids the wheel and builds against system libraries
item.technology: Python / Django / psycopg2 / PostgreSQL on Arch Linux

item.reason: The accepted answer identifies a single cause: the build container's default Docker network cannot resolve or reach the npm registry. It gives a concrete fix.
item.scenario:
A Node.js backend image fails to build on a CentOS Linux 8.1.1911 host running Docker 19.03.8 (build afacb8b). The Dockerfile is the standard pattern:
- FROM node:13
- WORKDIR /usr/src/app
- COPY package*.json ./
- RUN npm install
- COPY . .
- EXPOSE 8080
- CMD node server.js

The build always stops at the RUN npm install step with:

npm ERR! network timeout at: https://registry.npmjs.org/cookie/-/cookie-0.4.0.tgz

The dependencies are small and ordinary: express 4.17, body-parser, cors, config, consign, request 2.88 and xml2js. Nothing in package.json points to a private registry. item.root_cause: Containers launched during docker build on this host use Docker's default bridge network. From that network, DNS resolution and outbound access to registry.npmjs.org do not work, so npm's downloads time out.
item.fix: Run the build on the host's network stack so it uses the host's DNS and connectivity, for example: docker build -t cassiamani/nodeapp --network=host .
key_points: The failure is a Docker build networking/DNS problem, not a problem with npm or package.json
The default bridge network used by docker build cannot resolve or reach the npm registry
Building with --network=host uses the host's DNS and network, which resolves the timeout

The scenario does not reveal the fix or root cause beyond the observed npm network timeout, includes the key facts from the question, and the reference has one primary cause.

item.reason: Single identifiable root cause: leftover DOCKER_* environment variables from an old docker-machine/Toolbox setup, persisted in the shell rc file. sudo strips the user environment, which is why the sudo invocation works.
item.scenario:
Workstation: macOS 10.12.1 with zsh. I removed an older Docker install and did a clean install of the native Docker for Mac app, which uses hyperkit. There are no existing containers. The app's settings show it as running.

As my normal user, the client fails:
```
$ docker ps
Cannot connect to the Docker daemon. Is the docker daemon running on this host?
```
With sudo it works and prints an empty container list:
```
$ sudo docker ps
CONTAINER ID IMAGE COMMAND CREATED STATUS PORTS NAMES
```

What I've checked:
- In /usr/local/bin, docker, docker-compose, docker-machine and notary are symlinks into ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.docker/bin/.
- docker-machine-driver-xhyve is still linked from a Homebrew Cellar.
- `ps aux` shows com.docker.hyperkit and com.docker.driver.amd64-linux running as my own user.
- I ran `unset` on a few Docker-related shell variables in the current terminal. It made no lasting difference, and new terminals still fail.

item.root_cause: Leftover DOCKER_HOST, DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY, DOCKER_CERT_PATH and DOCKER_MACHINE_NAME exports from the old docker-machine setup are still in ~/.zshrc. They point the non-root client at a docker-machine endpoint that no longer exists instead of the local Docker for Mac socket. sudo drops the user's environment, so the root client uses the default socket and works.
item.fix: Remove the legacy DOCKER_* export lines from ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc), then restart the shell session. Running `unset` only affects the current shell, so the lines must be deleted from the rc file. `docker ps` then works without sudo.
key_points: Legacy DOCKER_HOST and related DOCKER_* variables from docker-machine/Toolbox are set in the user's environment
They are exported from a shell startup file (~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc), so unset in one session does not persist
sudo works because it does not carry over those user environment variables, so the default local socket is used
Fix: delete the entries from the rc file and open a new shell
item.technology: Docker for Mac / macOS shell environment

item.reason: Clear single root cause: the model's attribute cast truncates timestamps.
item.scenario:
We have a Laravel app on PostgreSQL with the TimescaleDB extension. An Eloquent query on the Measure model groups by `time` and sums two columns. It filters on operation_id 'ACC0000001', a time window of 2020-05-09 00:00 to 2020-05-10 00:00, source 'source1' and conso_prod 'Conso':

Measure::groupBy('time')->selectRaw('time, sum("delta") as sum_delta, sum("redistributed") as sum_redistr')->where(...)->get()

I dumped the SQL with toSql() and ran it by hand in pgAdmin. There it returns one row every 30 minutes, with time values incrementing as expected.

Through Eloquent, the collection has the same number of rows, but every row's `time` shows "2020-05-09 00:00". The sums look like they come back per row. The query text seems identical, so I can't see why the time values collapse to a single value only when the results come through the application.
item.root_cause: The Measure model's $casts declares 'time' => 'date'. Eloquent therefore casts each timestamp to a date and drops the time-of-day portion, so every row displays midnight of the same day. The database results themselves are correct.
item.fix: Change the model cast to 'time' => 'datetime' so Eloquent keeps the full timestamp.
key_points: The SQL and the database results are correct; the problem is in Eloquent's hydration of the model.
The model's $casts entry casts the time attribute to 'date'.
The 'date' cast truncates the time-of-day part, making every timestamp appear as 00:00.
Changing the cast to 'datetime' fixes it.

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer exactly: the model cast for time was 'date' and needed to be 'datetime'. The scenario preserves the key symptoms without mentioning casts, and the accepted answer identifies a single primary cause.

item.scenario: Developer environment: a Rails service is deployed into a local Minikube cluster (built and deployed with Skaffold). Locally, the team relies on pry breakpoints (`binding.pry`) dropped into controller code to inspect state interactively. Inside the cluster this no longer works. The operator attached to the running Rails pod and triggered the code path; the attached output shows pry starting to open a breakpoint session, but no prompt ever accepts input and the request just continues executing past the breakpoint as if it weren't there. The application otherwise runs fine and logs are visible through the attach session. The Deployment manifest is a fairly standard one with just image, name and labels on the container. Why does the breakpoint get skipped, and how can an interactive pry session be obtained in the pod?
item.root_cause: Kubernetes does not allocate a TTY or an open stdin for containers by default, so pry has no interactive terminal/input stream and immediately continues past the breakpoint.
item.fix: Add `stdin: true` and `tty: true` to the container spec in the Deployment YAML, redeploy, and then attach with `kubectl attach -it <pod_name>` to interact with the pry prompt.
key_points: Containers in Kubernetes get no TTY and no stdin by default
pry needs an interactive terminal/stdin, so it skips the breakpoint
Set stdin: true and tty: true in the container spec
Attach using kubectl attach -it

audit.notes: The item matches the accepted answer: Kubernetes containers lack stdin/TTY by default, causing pry to be non-interactive, and the fix is to set stdin:true and tty:true and attach with -it. item.reason: The thread is a deployment placement failure, and the accepted answer gives a cause: the scheduler reserves memory by the container soft limit, so the large reservations block placement of new tasks while old tasks still run. It also gives a concrete fix.
item.scenario:
We run an ECS cluster of three m5.large container instances, one in each of AZs A, B and C.

Service settings:
- REPLICA service, desired count 3
- Minimum healthy percent 30, maximum percent 100
- AZ balanced spread placement, no service autoscaling

Task definition settings:
- awsvpc network mode
- No task-level CPU or memory
- Container memory soft limit 2048 MB, no hard limit
- awslogs logging

The first start works: one container per instance. `docker stats` shows 230MiB / 7.501GiB. The ECS console shows each instance with Memory Registered 7680 / Available 5632 and CPU 2048 / 2048.

When Jenkins triggers a force-new-deployment, the job reports Success, but the old code keeps running. The deployment events show:

"(service App-V1-Service) was unable to place a task because no container instance met all of its requirements. The closest matching (container-instance 90d4ba21-...) has insufficient memory available."

Actual memory usage on every host is very low. I had already dropped minimum healthy percent to 30, hoping ECS would stop old containers before starting new ones, but placement still fails. Why can't the new tasks be scheduled?
item.root_cause: The ECS scheduler places tasks by the reserved memory (the 2048 MB container soft limit), not by actual usage. During the rolling deployment the old tasks still hold their 2048 MB reservations, so the reservations needed for the new tasks exceed the instances' registered available memory and placement fails.
item.fix: Lower the container soft limit (memoryReservation) to about 1 GB or less. The container can still use more memory when needed, and old and new tasks can then coexist during deployment. Alternatively, keep the 2048 MB reservation and lower the minimum healthy percent so old tasks are stopped first, freeing reservations.
key_points: ECS placement uses the memoryReservation (soft limit) reserved per container, not actual memory usage
During deployment, old tasks' reservations plus new tasks' reservations exceed available instance memory (5632 MB available per instance)
Reduce the soft limit to ≤1 GB, or reduce minimum healthy percent so old tasks are stopped before new ones are placed

audit.notes: The item closely matches the accepted answer: ECS accounts for the container soft memory limit as reserved memory during deployment, causing placement failure despite low actual usage; lowering the soft limit or changing deployment settings is the stated fix. The scenario includes the memory numbers and error but does not explicitly state the reservation-based scheduling cause. The original evidence is present, and the accepted answer identifies one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear single root cause: the registry is not listed as insecure in the daemon config, so the daemon insists on HTTPS against a plain-HTTP registry.
item.scenario:
I'm on Windows with Docker Toolbox, using the boot2docker VM under VirtualBox at 192.168.99.100. I deployed a private registry container on port 5000 by following the official "deploying a registry" guide.

Pulling from it fails:

```

Using default tag: latest
Error response from daemon: Get https://192.168.99.100:5000/v2/: http: server gave HTTP response to HTTPS client
```

The same steps work fine on a Mac.

Relevant parts of `docker info`:
- Server Version: 17.06.0-ce
- Operating System: Boot2Docker 17.06.0-ce (TCL 7.2)
- Kernel 4.4.74-boot2docker
- Storage Driver: aufs
- Labels: provider=virtualbox
- Registry: https://index.docker.io/v1/
- Insecure Registries: 127.0.0.0/8
- Debug Mode (server): true

I suspect something on the client side is misconfigured. What is causing the HTTPS/HTTP mismatch, and how do I fix it?

item.fix: Add "insecure-registries":["192.168.99.100:5000"] to the Docker daemon's daemon.json (C:\ProgramData\Docker\config\daemon.json on Windows, /etc/docker/daemon.json on Linux). Then restart the Docker daemon.

The daemon's Insecure Registries list only contains 127.0.0.0/8, so 192.168.99.100:5000 is not trusted for HTTP
Add 192.168.99.100:5000 to insecure-registries in the daemon.json config
Restart the Docker daemon for the change to take effect

item.scenario:
On a macOS dev machine (Python 2.7), a Django app uses django-haystack with the Elasticsearch backend. Running `./manage.py rebuild_index` and confirming the wipe prompt produces this output:

Removing all documents from your index because you said so.

Ensure the HAYSTACK_CONNECTIONS URL matches the working Elasticsearch endpoint

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: HFS+ lacks sparse file support, so a write into a large ftruncate-extended file forces zero-filling of a large region.
item.scenario: We run an alpha build of a database's on-disk virtual memory feature, which moves rarely used objects out to a swap file. It is stable on Linux. On Mac OS X Snow Leopard, the process sometimes goes into uninterruptible wait (D state) for several minutes. When this happens it is inside either fseeko() or fwrite() on the swap file. Each write is tiny, about 256 bytes. Eventually the call returns and the process carries on normally, with no crash and no error. How the swap file is set up: at startup it is opened with fopen() and then grown to about 26 GB with ftruncate(). It is then unlink()ed so the space is freed when the process exits, while the open handle stays in use. Writes go to various offsets inside that 26 GB range. Why would a tiny write block for minutes on macOS but not on Linux?
item.root_cause: HFS+ has very poor support for sparse files. A write at an offset inside the large, never-written region created by ftruncate() makes the filesystem materialize (zero-fill) a large part of the file on disk, and the process blocks in uninterruptible I/O while that happens.
item.fix: Don't preallocate the whole 26 GB file with one ftruncate. If writes are linear (replacing existing blocks or appending at a free-space pointer), extend the file in smaller, more frequent ftruncate steps so each expansion only initializes a small amount and the pauses stay short.
key_points: HFS+ on macOS does not handle sparse files well, unlike Linux filesystems
The 26 GB file created via ftruncate is sparse/unwritten
Writing at an offset in it makes HFS+ zero-fill or materialize a large portion of the file, so the small write blocks for minutes
Mitigation: grow the file incrementally with smaller ftruncate calls and write linearly
item.technology: macOS HFS+ filesystem / C file I/O (Redis VM)

audit.notes: The root cause matches the accepted answer: HFS+ poor sparse-file behavior causing large materialization/initialization on small writes into a large ftruncate-created file. The suggested mitigation of smaller, more frequent ftruncate expansions is directly from the accepted answer, though it was phrased there as conditional/speculative. The scenario includes the necessary ftruncate/large-file details but does not explicitly name sparse files or HFS+ as the cause. An experienced engineer could infer it from the macOS/HFS+/large ftruncate/tiny write symptoms. The accepted answer centers on one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear single root cause: the host path is not shared into the Docker VM on Windows, so the bind mount comes up empty.
item.scenario: I'm containerizing a small Node.js app and want its tests to run every time the container starts. The Dockerfile is based on node:4-onbuild, sets WORKDIR /usr/src/app, and uses CMD ["npm","test"]. I built it with `docker build -t myapp .`. I then ran it with a bind mount of my project folder, trying several path styles: `-v //c/Project/nodejs/my-app:/usr/src/app`, `-v /c/Project/nodejs/my-app:/usr/src/app`, and `-v c:/Project/nodejs/my-app:/usr/src/app`. Every attempt fails the same way. npm 2.15.9 on node v4.5.0 (kernel 4.4.15-moby) reports `ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/usr/src/app/package.json'`, as if the mounted directory were empty. If I use COPY in the Dockerfile instead of a volume, the files show up and the tests run fine. Host is Windows 10 with Docker 1.12.0. Why does the mounted directory appear empty in the container?
item.root_cause: On Windows, Docker runs inside a Linux VM, and bind mounts resolve against that VM's filesystem. Only C:\Users is shared into the VM (as /c/Users), so /c/Project doesn't exist there and Docker mounts an empty directory. COPY works because the build context is sent to the engine over the API rather than mounted.
item.fix: Move the project under C:\Users (for example C:\Users\<name>\...) and bind mount it using the /c/Users/... path. Alternatively, share the drive or folder with the Docker VM.
key_points: Docker for Windows containers run in a Linux VM; -v host paths refer to the VM filesystem
Only C:\Users is shared into the VM by default (as /c/Users)
Mounting a nonexistent host path yields an empty directory, hence the missing package.json
COPY works because the build context is sent over the API, not via a volume mount

audit.notes: The root cause and main fix match the accepted answer: Docker for Windows uses a Linux VM, only C:\Users is shared as /c/Users, so /c/Project is nonexistent in the VM and mounts empty; COPY works via build context transfer. The scenario includes the necessary evidence without explicitly giving away the cause. The accepted answer identifies one primary cause.

- cable/config.ru sets allowed_request_origins to `http://localhost:3000`.

Why do subscriptions work in dev but never get established on Heroku?
item.root_cause: The production ActionCable host and URL point at the herokuapp.com domain, but browsers load the app from the custom domain. The client's websocket connection and subscription therefore never succeed, so broadcasts reach no subscriber.
item.fix: Set an env var with the real public host, e.g. `heroku config:set RAILS_HOST=www.example.com`. Then in production.rb set `config.action_cable.url = "wss://#{ENV['RAILS_HOST']}/cable"` so the cable URL matches the domain clients actually use.
key_points: Clients reach the app via a custom domain, not app-name.herokuapp.com.
The ActionCable URL/host config references the herokuapp.com domain, so subscriptions are never established even though broadcasts are logged.
The fix is to point config.action_cable.url (wss://.../cable) at the custom domain, e.g. via a RAILS_HOST env var.
