item.reason: The thread has a single identifiable cause. The disk sits outside the node resource group, so the AKS identity lacks permissions on it, and the 403 error is enough evidence to reach that diagnosis.
item.scenario:
We're setting up a MySQL deployment on AKS that uses a pre-created managed Azure Disk, following the static Azure Disk volume guide. The pod spec mounts an azureDisk volume as follows: diskName PHIO_DB_VOL, diskURI /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<my-grp>/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/PHIO_DB_VOL, kind Managed, mountPath /var/lib/mysql.

After running kubectl apply, the pod is scheduled to aks-nodepool1-...-vmss000001 but never starts. kubectl describe shows these events:

Warning FailedAttachVolume (x23 over 31m) attachdetach-controller AttachVolume.Attach failed for volume "dbvolume" : compute.DisksClient#Get: Failure responding to request: StatusCode=403 ... Code="AuthorizationFailed" Message="The client '<GUID>' with object id '<same GUID>' does not have authorization to perform action 'Microsoft.Compute/disks/read' over scope '/subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<my-grp>/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/PHIO_DB_VOL' or the scope is invalid."

Warning FailedMount kubelet ... timeout expired waiting for volumes to attach or mount ... list of unattached volumes=[dbvolume default-token-...]

As far as we can tell, we followed every step of the guide. We can't find any additional parameter that the YAML is missing.
item.root_cause: The managed disk was created in a resource group other than the AKS node resource group (MC_*). The cluster's service principal or managed identity has no RBAC permissions on that group, so its Microsoft.Compute/disks/read call returns 403.
item.fix:
Choose one of these options:
- Create the disk in the AKS node resource group.
- Grant the cluster's service principal or managed identity an RBAC role on the disk's resource group. This can be Contributor, Storage Account Contributor, or a custom role with Microsoft.Compute/disks/read and write.
key_points: The disk resides outside the AKS-managed node resource group
The AKS cluster identity (service principal or managed identity) lacks RBAC on the disk's resource group
The 403 AuthorizationFailed on Microsoft.Compute/disks/read comes from the cluster's identity, not from the pod
The fix is to put the disk in the node resource group or grant Contributor (or disks read/write) on the disk's resource group
item.technology: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) / Azure Managed Disks

audit.notes: The root cause and fixes match the accepted answer: AKS identity lacks permissions to read/manage a disk outside the node resource group, and the remedies are to use the node resource group or grant suitable RBAC. The scenario leaks a major part of the cause because the event explicitly says AuthorizationFailed and lacks Microsoft.Compute/disks/read permission. Despite that, it is solvable from the included 403 authorization error and disk scope. The accepted answer centers on one primary issue: missing permissions for the AKS identity on the disk resource group.

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: the JBoss managed connection pool is exhausted. The accepted answer points to the default max-pool-size or to connection leaks.
item.scenario:
Our web app runs on JBoss AS 6 with Hibernate 3.6, PostgreSQL 9.0 and the postgresql-9.0-802.jdbc4 driver. A HornetQ MDB consumes health messages from about 60 remote standalone Java nodes, each sending one message every 120 seconds. For each message the MDB parses it, runs a few DB lookups and writes to several tables. As we added more nodes, the app started losing database access. The log shows:

ERROR [org.hibernate.util.JDBCExceptionReporter] (Thread-100 (group:HornetQ-client-global-threads-...)) Unable to get managed connection for webAppDatasource; - nested throwable: (javax.resource.ResourceException: Unable to get managed connection for webAppDatasource)

Quartz jobs then fail with EJBTransactionRolledbackException: GenericJDBCException: Cannot open connection. Deeper in the trace: "No ManagedConnections available within configured blocking timeout ( 30000 [ms] )" from InternalManagedConnectionPool.getConnection.

After this the whole app is unusable. To recover I pause the queue, clear the backlog and restart PostgreSQL.

What we've tried:
- Added c3p0 with default settings.
- Moved the DB to its own server.
- Added autoReconnect, maxReconnects, failOverReadOnly and check-valid-connection-sql to the local-tx-datasource. It defines only jndi-name, connection-url, driver-class, user and password plus those options.

Normally the app seems to use about 4-5 connections.
item.root_cause: The JBoss JCA managed connection pool for webAppDatasource is exhausted. All pooled connections are in use, either because the default max-pool-size of 20 is too small for the MDB load or because connections are leaked and never closed. New requests block for the 30 s blocking timeout and then fail.
item.fix: Increase max-pool-size on the JBoss datasource above the default of 20. Also check the code for connection leaks and make sure every connection is explicitly closed or returned to the pool.
key_points: The error means the JBoss connection pool is exhausted (No ManagedConnections available within the 30000 ms blocking timeout).
The datasource sets no max-pool-size, so the JBoss default of 20 applies.
The remedy is to raise max-pool-size or find leaked connections that are not being closed.
autoReconnect, c3p0 and validation SQL do not address pool exhaustion.
item.technology: JBoss AS 6 / JCA datasource with Hibernate and PostgreSQL JDBC

audit.notes: The accepted answer explicitly identifies JBoss connection pool exhaustion and recommends increasing max-pool-size or checking for leaked/unclosed connections, so the root cause and fix are faithful. However, the scenario includes the decisive trace text 'No ManagedConnections available within configured blocking timeout', which strongly reveals the pool-exhaustion cause, so no_leak is false. The scenario is solvable because it includes the key stack trace and context. The accepted answer has one primary root cause: exhausted connection pool, with two possible reasons/remediations.

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: Kestrel bound to localhost inside the container, so Docker's port forwarding can't reach it; fix is binding to 0.0.0.0.
item.scenario:
On a Mac I'm containerizing a basic ASP.NET demo built from the yo aspnet 'Empty Application' template. Running it directly with `dnx web` works: Kestrel prints 'Hosting environment: Production / Now listening on: http://localhost:5000 / Application started' and the browser shows 'Hello World!' at http://localhost:5000.

Inside Docker it doesn't work. The image builds fine. The Dockerfile has `EXPOSE 5000` and I start the container with `docker run -i -t -p 5000:5000 container_name`. Kestrel prints the same startup lines, including 'Now listening on: http://localhost:5000'. But http://localhost:5000 in the browser gives ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED.

Docker reports it is using the default machine at 192.168.99.100. http://192.168.99.100:5000 also returns ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED. `docker inspect container_name | grep IPAddress` shows the container IP is 172.17.0.2. Browsing http://172.17.0.2:5000 just spins and then times out. How do I reach the app from my browser?
item.root_cause: Kestrel inside the container listens only on localhost (http://localhost:5000). Traffic forwarded by Docker's port mapping does not arrive on the container's loopback interface, so nothing answers it. The container IP 172.17.0.2 is not reachable from the Mac. The correct address is the Docker VM at 192.168.99.100.
item.fix: Make Kestrel bind to all interfaces by changing the Dockerfile entrypoint to `ENTRYPOINT ["dnx", "web", "--server.urls", "http://0.0.0.0:5000"]`. Then run with a port mapping such as `-p 80:5000` and browse to the VM IP, http://192.168.99.100.
key_points: Kestrel is bound to localhost inside the container, so it is unreachable through Docker's forwarded port
The server must listen on 0.0.0.0 (for example via --server.urls http://0.0.0.0:5000)
On Mac with docker-machine, browse to the VM IP 192.168.99.100, not localhost and not the container IP 172.17.0.2
The -p port mapping is what links host and container ports; EXPOSE alone is not sufficient

audit.notes: The item accurately reflects the accepted answer: Kestrel must bind to 0.0.0.0 inside the container and the browser should use the Docker VM IP with an appropriate port mapping. The scenario includes the original diagnostic evidence without explicitly giving away the fix. An experienced engineer could infer the bind-address issue from the Kestrel localhost log plus Docker port forwarding behavior. The accepted answer identifies one main root cause/fix path rather than multiple competing causes.

item.reason: Clear single root cause: config file from newer Redis (2.6) used with older Redis binary (2.2 from Ubuntu repo) that doesn't support tcp-keepalive directive.
item.scenario:
On an Ubuntu 12.04 host (EC2 base AMI), redis-server was installed with apt-get. It refuses to start. The startup output shows:

*** FATAL CONFIG FILE ERROR ***
Reading the configuration file, at line 56
>>> 'tcp-keepalive 0'
Bad directive or wrong number of arguments

The config file in use is the full commented example redis.conf. It has daemonize no, pidfile /var/run/redis.pid, port 6379, timeout 0, a long commented 'TCP keepalive' section ending in 'tcp-keepalive 0', then loglevel notice, logfile stdout, databases 16, and the snapshotting section. The line looks syntactically correct: one directive and one numeric argument, matching the comments above it. Nobody has hand-edited the file in a way that would explain a typo. item.fix: Comment out or delete the tcp-keepalive line. Another option is to use the example config file that matches the installed Redis version. Or upgrade Redis to a newer version, for example from the rwky/redis PPA, which installs 2.8.x.
key_points: Installed Redis version (2.2.x from Ubuntu apt) is older than the config file's version (2.6 example)
tcp-keepalive directive is not supported in older Redis (2.2/2.4)
Check the version with dpkg -s redis-server and match the config to it, or remove the line / upgrade Redis

The scenario includes the relevant symptoms and environment without explicitly naming the version mismatch or old Redis version, so it remains solvable without directly leaking the answer. item.reason: Clear single root cause: Redis server has no requirepass configured while the client sends AUTH; evidence (error message, redis-cli -a working, monitor showing nothing) supports diagnosis without revealing it.
item.scenario:
Our Java service uses Jedis 2.8.0 with a connection pool built like this:

```
jedisPool = new JedisPool(jedisPoolConfig, host, port, IDLE_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT, authSecret);
```

Whenever the app borrows a connection from the pool, it throws:

```
Caused by: redis.clients.jedis.exceptions.JedisDataException: ERR Client sent AUTH, but no password is set
 at redis.clients.jedis.Protocol.processError(Protocol.java:123)
 ...
 at redis.clients.jedis.BinaryJedis.auth(BinaryJedis.java:2049)
 at redis.clients.jedis.JedisFactory.makeObject(JedisFactory.java:89)
 at org.apache.commons.pool2.impl.GenericObjectPool.create(GenericObjectPool.java:868)
 ...
 at redis.clients.util.Pool.getResource(Pool.java:49)
```

What we have already checked:
- Running `redis-cli -a <same password>` against the same host and port works, and commands succeed.
- We logged the password value passed into JedisPool. It matches the expected secret exactly.
- We ran `redis-cli monitor` on the Redis instance while reproducing the error, and no AUTH command appears in the output.

We need to know why the pool cannot authenticate when the CLI can, and how to get connections working.
item.root_cause: The Redis instance has no password configured (requirepass is not set). Redis therefore rejects the AUTH command that Jedis sends when the pool is created with a password. redis-cli -a only seemed to work because the server ignored the password.
item.fix: Either set a password on the server by adding the requirepass option to the Redis configuration file and restarting Redis, or create the JedisPool without the password argument, e.g. new JedisPool(jedisPoolConfig, host, port, IDLE_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT).
key_points: Redis server has no requirepass/password configured
Jedis sends AUTH because a password is passed to JedisPool, and the server rejects it
redis-cli -a success is misleading; the password is just ignored
Fix: set requirepass in the Redis config and restart, or drop the password from the JedisPool constructor

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer exactly. However, the scenario includes the Redis error message 'ERR Client sent AUTH, but no password is set,' which directly states/strongly reveals the root cause, so no_leak is false. The scenario is otherwise solvable and the reference has one primary cause.

item.reason: The thread describes one concrete failure: Delve cannot launch its process inside a container. The accepted answer ties it to the container's default privilege restrictions and fixes it by running the container with --privileged.
item.scenario:
I'm setting up remote debugging of a Go program from my editor (Atom) into a Docker container. Docker runs on a Mac host, and the debugger is Delve inside the container. In a shell in the container, I installed Delve with `go get github.com/derekparker/delve/cmd/dlv`. Running `dlv debug hello.go` in /go/src/app fails immediately with:

```
could not launch process: fork/exec ./debug: operation not permitted
```

I'm already root in the container. Trying `sudo` just gives `bash: sudo: command not found`. Because Delve on macOS normally needs code signing, I codesigned on the Mac host as well. That changed nothing, and I wouldn't expect host signing to matter inside a Linux container anyway. The program builds fine, so only launching it under the debugger fails. What is blocking Delve, and how do I get it working inside the container?
item.root_cause: The container runs with Docker's default restricted privileges. These block the operations Delve needs to launch and trace the debug binary, so fork/exec fails with 'operation not permitted' even for root inside the container. Host-side macOS code signing is unrelated.
item.fix: Start the container with `docker run --privileged ...` so Delve has the privileges it needs to launch and debug the process.
key_points: The error comes from Docker's default container security restrictions, not missing root or sudo inside the container
Codesigning on the macOS host doesn't affect a Linux container
Running the container with --privileged resolves the error

The scenario includes the relevant evidence without explicitly naming --privileged or the exact root cause. item.reason: Clear diagnosis: the Debian archive signing key is missing from apt's trusted keyring, which causes a NO_PUBKEY error, and the answer gives a concrete fix.
item.scenario:
On a Debian etch server, running `apt-get update` appears to finish. It fetches the Release.gpg and Release files from ftp.us.debian.org, hits all the Sources/Packages indexes, and prints 'Fetched 68.8kB in 1s'. It then ends with these warnings:

```
W: There is no public key available for the following key IDs:
9AA38DCD55BE302B
W: GPG error: http://ftp.us.debian.org etch Release: The following signatures couldn't be verified because the public key is not available: NO_PUBKEY 9AA38DCD55BE302B
W: You may want to run apt-get update to correct these problems
```

Running `apt-get update` again gives exactly the same warnings, so the suggested remedy loops back on itself. The repository itself is reachable and the index files download fine. The operator wants to know why the warnings persist and how to clear them so packages from the archive are trusted.
item.root_cause: apt's trusted keyring (/etc/apt/trusted.gpg) lacks the public key 9AA38DCD55BE302B that signed the etch Release file. apt therefore cannot verify the Release signature, and re-running apt-get update does not add the key.
item.fix: Run `apt-key update` to refresh the keyring from the Debian archive keyring, then run apt-get update again. If that fails, fetch the key with `gpg --keyserver wwwkeys.eu.pgp.net --recv-keys 9AA38DCD55BE302B`, import it with `apt-key add /root/.gnupg/pubring.gpg`, and rerun apt-get update.
key_points: The NO_PUBKEY error means the archive signing key is missing from apt's trusted keyring
apt-get update itself does not install or refresh signing keys
apt-key manages the secure-apt keyring in /etc/apt/trusted.gpg
Fix by running apt-key update, or by fetching key 9AA38DCD55BE302B from a keyserver and adding it with apt-key add

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: missing apt trusted key and use apt-key update or manually fetch/add the key. However, the scenario includes the exact NO_PUBKEY/public-key warnings, which strongly reveal the root cause.

item.reason: Clear dpkg file conflict with identifiable cause (leftover Ubuntu runc package conflicting with containerd.io) and concrete fix.
item.scenario:
Ubuntu 16.04 desktop running docker-ce had been working until unattended updates ran a few days ago. Now `docker ps` returns: "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock. Is the docker daemon running?"

Followed the official docker-ce removal/reinstall steps; no change. `sudo apt-get install docker-ce` reports docker-ce 5:18.09.0~3-0~ubuntu-xenial is already newest, but: "docker-ce : Depends: containerd.io but it is not going to be installed" and suggests `apt-get -f install`.

Running `sudo apt-get -f install` tries to install containerd.io 1.2.0-1 and fails during unpack:
"dpkg: error processing archive /var/cache/apt/archives/containerd.io_1.2.0-1_amd64.deb (--unpack): trying to overwrite '/usr/sbin/runc', which is also in package runc 1.0.0~rc2+docker1.13.1-0ubuntu1~16.04.1"
followed by "Sub-process /usr/bin/dpkg returned an error code (1)".

As a debugging step I manually deleted /usr/sbin/runc (ls now says it doesn't exist), but the -f install fails exactly the same way. Looking for next steps.
item.root_cause: An old Ubuntu-packaged `runc` (1.0.0~rc2+docker1.13.1), left over from a past legacy Docker install, is still registered with dpkg as owning /usr/sbin/runc, so the new containerd.io package (which ships its own runc) cannot unpack and docker-ce stays unconfigured. Deleting the file doesn't help because dpkg's package ownership remains.
item.fix: Remove docker-ce first (`apt-get remove docker-ce`), then remove the old package (`apt-get remove runc`), then reinstall with `apt-get install docker-ce`, which pulls in containerd.io cleanly.
key_points: The conflict is a dpkg package ownership clash between the old 'runc' package and containerd.io over /usr/sbin/runc
The runc package is a leftover from an old, unsupported docker 1.13.1 install
Manually deleting the file is ineffective; the runc package must be removed via apt
docker-ce must be removed before runc can be removed, then docker-ce reinstalled

audit.notes: The item matches the accepted answer: remove the old runc package, possibly after removing docker-ce, then reinstall docker-ce/containerd.io. The scenario, however, includes the dpkg error explicitly naming package runc 1.0.0~rc2+docker1.13.1 as owning /usr/sbin/runc, which strongly hints at the root cause. The scenario is solvable from the provided evidence, and the reference has one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: the MySQL error comes from user/host grants, not from networking. The accepted answer names one root cause and gives a fix.
item.scenario:
We run MySQL server inside a VirtualBox guest (NAT networking). We need to reach it from a client on the host machine. NAT port forwarding for the MySQL port is configured and verified. Every connection attempt from the host, whatever the client tool, fails with the same message:

```
Host '10.0.2.2' is not allowed to connect to this MySQL server
```

We are trying to log in as root. In my.cnf we confirmed these lines are present:
```
skip-external-locking
bind-address = 0.0.0.0
```
The error did not change. We also tried `bind-address = 10.0.2.2`, but then the MySQL service failed to start at all, so we reverted it. Connections from inside the VM work. What is preventing the host from connecting?
item.root_cause: The server is reachable over the network. The root account is only defined for localhost, which is the default on most installs. The mysql.user table has no row whose Host value (such as '%' or '10.0.2.2') matches the client address 10.0.2.2, so the server rejects the connection.
item.fix: Run `select user,host from mysql.user where user='root';` to check the current entries. Then create a root account for the client host and grant it privileges: `create user 'root'@'10.0.2.2' identified by 'pw'; grant all privileges on *.* to 'root'@'10.0.2.2' with grant option; flush privileges;`.
key_points: The error is an authentication/authorization rejection, not a network or bind-address problem
Root is localhost-only by default; mysql.user has no Host entry matching 10.0.2.2 or %
Create or grant a user for 'root'@'10.0.2.2' (or '%') and flush privileges
bind-address must be a local interface address; 10.0.2.2 is the NAT gateway/host side, so the server could not start with it

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: MySQL grants lack a root entry matching host 10.0.2.2, and the remedy is to inspect mysql.user and create/grant root@10.0.2.2. The scenario includes the key error and context without explicitly stating the grant-table cause. It is solvable from the presented evidence and has one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear single root cause: the Subsystem sftp path doesn't exist on CentOS 7 (Debian-style path), which gives exit status 127.
item.scenario:
A CentOS 7 VPS accepts interactive SSH logins for 'user' without trouble, but SFTP sessions to the same host fail. The client is a Mac running OpenSSH_6.9p1/LibreSSL 2.1.8, and the server reports OpenSSH_6.6.1. Running `sftp -v user@example.org` shows the connection being established and authentication succeeding. After that the session closes, and the client reports exit status 127.

The sshd_config came from a template. Relevant lines:
```
Port 22
Protocol 2
UsePrivilegeSeparation yes
PermitRootLogin no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
PasswordAuthentication yes
X11Forwarding no
AcceptEnv LANG LC_*
#Subsystem sftp /usr/lib/openssh/sftp-server
Subsystem sftp /usr/lib/openssh/sftp-server
UsePAM yes
AllowUsers user@xx.xxx.xx.xxx user@xx.xxx.xx.xxx apt-dater@xx.xxx.xx.xxx
Match User user
 PasswordAuthentication yes
```

The user is allowed by AllowUsers, and the same credentials work for a normal shell. Only the file transfer subsystem fails.
item.root_cause: The Subsystem sftp directive points to /usr/lib/openssh/sftp-server, a Debian-style path that does not exist on this CentOS server. When sshd tries to execute it, the command is not found, giving exit status 127.
item.fix: Change the Subsystem directive to the server's actual sftp-server path (on CentOS, typically /usr/libexec/openssh/sftp-server), or use `Subsystem sftp internal-sftp`. Then restart sshd.
key_points: Exit status 127 means the command executed for the sftp subsystem was not found
The Subsystem sftp path /usr/lib/openssh/sftp-server does not exist on the server
Fix by pointing Subsystem at an existing sftp-server binary or using internal-sftp, then restart sshd

audit.notes: The accepted answer identifies the missing/nonexistent sftp-server path in the Subsystem directive and suggests using an existing path or internal-sftp. The item’s CentOS-specific path is an implementation detail but consistent with the accepted answer and scenario. The scenario includes the relevant config path and symptoms but does not explicitly state that the path is invalid. The evidence is sufficient for an experienced engineer to infer the cause, and the reference centers on one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: the connected subnet route is configured via a gateway instead of as on-link, so the gateway is unreachable.
item.scenario:
On a dual-homed Linux test server, adding a static route out of the internal interface fails. Interfaces: eth0 is 192.168.36.132 with mask 255.255.254.0, and eth1 is a public 116.x.x.x/26 address that carries the default route.

Command run:
`route add -net 10.248.12.0 netmask 255.255.255.240 gw 192.168.36.254 dev eth0`

It returns: `SIOCADDRT: Network is unreachable`

`ip route list` shows:
```
116.66.240.64/26 dev eth1 proto kernel scope link src 116.xx.xx.xx
192.168.238.0/24 via 192.168.36.254 dev eth0
192.168.239.0/24 via 192.168.36.254 dev eth0
192.168.36.0/23 via 192.168.36.254 dev eth0
169.254.0.0/16 dev eth0 scope link
127.0.0.0/8 dev lo scope link
default via 116.xx.xx.xx dev eth1
```
`netstat -anr` agrees. It lists 192.168.36.0/255.255.254.0 with gateway 192.168.36.254 and flags UG on eth0.

The operator has spent several days on this and cannot work out why the kernel rejects the 192.168.36.254 gateway. That address sits inside eth0's own address range.
item.root_cause: The 192.168.36.0/23 network that eth0 sits on is routed via gateway 192.168.36.254 instead of being a directly connected (scope link) route. As a result the kernel has no on-link route to reach 192.168.36.254 itself. Any route that uses it as a next hop is therefore rejected as unreachable.
item.fix: Delete the gateway-based route for 192.168.36.0/23. Replace it with a directly connected route, for example `ip route add 192.168.36.0/23 dev eth0` (shown as scope link, flags U, gateway 0.0.0.0). Then re-add the static route via 192.168.36.254.
key_points: The 192.168.36.0/23 route is wrongly marked UG via 192.168.36.254 instead of being a link-local (scope link) route
With no on-link route for that subnet, the kernel cannot reach the gateway 192.168.36.254 as a neighbour, so it reports SIOCADDRT Network is unreachable
The fix is to replace the gateway route with `ip route add 192.168.36.0/23 dev eth0` (no gateway)

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: the eth0 subnet route is incorrectly via 192.168.36.254 rather than a directly connected scope-link route, making the next hop unreachable. item.reason: Accepted answer identifies a specific root cause: the test traffic targeted the gateway's own public IP, which is not part of HOME_NET, so rules written as EXTERNAL_NET -> HOME_NET never matched.
item.scenario:
Our home gateway runs Snort in inline mode through NFQUEUE. Four Snort processes read queues 0-3 via an iptables rule: `NFQUEUE balance 0:3 bypass cpu-fanout`. New inbound TCP/80 connections from one allowed remote host jump to a chain that NFLOGs and then queues them. Established traffic is sent to Snort through a separate chain.

Rules come from Emerging Threats via pulledpork. One example is sid:2017590, the D-Link backdoor User-Agent rule:

`alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET $HTTP_PORTS (... content:"xmlset_roodkcableoj28840ybtide"; http_header; ...)`

To test it, lighttpd was started on the gateway itself, listening on port 80 of its WAN interface. From a remote host I ran:

`curl -A 'xmlset_roodkcableoj28840ybtide' 'http://<EXTERNAL_IP>'`

The page comes back immediately and Snort logs no alert. The iptables counters show packets hitting the NFQUEUE rule, so Snort is receiving traffic.

During BitTorrent load, only the Snort processes on CPUs 1 and 2 get busy, while those on CPUs 0 and 3 stay idle. I have already reviewed the iptables/NFQUEUE setup, the systemd units and the alert output, and found nothing obviously wrong.
item.root_cause: The test traffic was aimed at the gateway's own public IP, which is not part of $HOME_NET (only the LAN subnets are). Rules written as $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET therefore never match that traffic, so Snort processes the packets but raises no alert.
item.fix: Test against a host or address inside the defined HOME_NET, such as a LAN server reached through the gateway. Alternatively, include the gateway's public IP in HOME_NET if traffic to the gateway itself should be inspected.
key_points: Snort is receiving packets; the issue is rule matching, not packet delivery
The rule's direction is $EXTERNAL_NET -> $HOME_NET
The gateway's own public/WAN IP is not part of HOME_NET (only LAN subnets are)
Traffic to the gateway's public IP does not match the rule, so the testing method is at fault
item.technology: Snort inline IPS with iptables NFQUEUE

item.reason: The thread describes a concrete diagnosis problem: read errors that disappear on their own. The accepted answer explains the mechanism, which is pending sectors being remapped once they are overwritten.
item.scenario:
A small Arch Linux server keeps most of its data on an md RAID-1 (md16) built from two SATA disks. After about 4 months of normal service, the kernel log began showing repeated read failures on one member, sdd. Typical entries:

```
ata5.01: failed command: READ DMA EXT
... Emask 0x9 (media error)
ata5.01: error: { UNC }
sd 4:0:1:0: [sdd] Sense Key : Medium Error [current]
sd 4:0:1:0: [sdd] Add. Sense: Unrecovered read error - auto reallocate failed
end_request: I/O error, dev sdd, sector 657746444
md/raid1:md16: read error corrected (8 sectors at 657744392 on sdd1)
md/raid1:md16: redirecting sector 657742336 to other mirror: sdd1
```

Each error named a different sector and caused a multi-second stall. They appeared mostly during backups, but also on roughly every fifth save of a small text file.

smartctl on sdd reports:
- Raw_Read_Error_Rate raw 1606
- Reallocated_Sector_Ct 0
- Reallocated_Event_Count 0
- Current_Pending_Sector 51

A replacement disk was ordered. A day later the errors stopped completely. There was no reboot and nothing was changed. Later the disk was removed from the array and re-added, and it still behaves normally. Why did the errors stop?
item.root_cause: A physical region of the platter went bad. The drive flagged those sectors as pending, but it could not remap them while they still held data, so every read of them failed. Once the sectors were overwritten (md rewriting the data from the good mirror, or the resync), the drive remapped them to spare sectors and the read errors stopped.
item.fix: Overwrite the bad sectors so the drive can remap them, for example via md's correction from the mirror, a RAID resync, or zeroing/reformatting the disk. After that, monitor SMART reallocated and pending counts, and replace the disk if more of the surface starts to fail.
key_points: Unreadable sectors are marked pending (Current_Pending_Sector) but cannot be remapped while they hold data that can't be read
Writing to or overwriting those sectors lets the drive remap them to spares
md RAID-1 rewrites failed sectors from the other mirror, and a re-add/resync overwrites the disk, which triggered the remapping
After remapping, the errors stop unless more media fails, so the drive should still be monitored
item.technology: Linux md RAID / SATA HDD SMART

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: bad physical sectors could not be remapped while containing unreadable data, but overwriting/rebuilding allowed remapping and stopped the read errors. The scenario includes diagnostic evidence such as pending sectors and auto-reallocate failure but does not explicitly give away the explanation. It is solvable from the logs/SMART data, and the accepted answer presents one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: system resolver (mDNSResponder) behaves differently from nslookup/dig, and its DNS server ordering sends queries to ISP servers that don't know internal names.
item.scenario:
After upgrading a MacBook to Mac OS X 10.6 (Darwin 10.0.0, OpenSSH 5.2p1), I can no longer reach internal hosts by short name. I cleared out ~/.ssh in case it was a config or known_hosts problem, and nothing changed.

nslookup works:
```
~: nslookup nevada
Server: 10.94.62.3
Address: 10.94.62.3#53
Name: nevada.example.com
Address: 10.94.62.3
```
ssh to the same name fails:
```
~: ssh nevada
ssh: Could not resolve hostname nevada: nodename nor servname provided, or not known
```
The failure is intermittent. Other apps sometimes fail to resolve internal names too. The network settings come from the office DHCP. DHCP hands out the internal DNS server (10.94.62.3) and also the ISP's public DNS servers. Internal names are served only by the internal server, which uses split DNS. Why does nslookup resolve the host while ssh and other applications don't?
item.root_cause: On Snow Leopard, normal applications resolve names through mDNSResponder, while nslookup and dig query /etc/resolv.conf directly via BIND. mDNSResponder sometimes changes the order of the configured DNS servers. When it queries the ISP DNS servers first, it gets no internal record, or the public IP under split DNS, and resolution fails.
item.fix: Configure only the required internal DNS server(s) in the Mac's DNS settings. If needed, remove the ISP DNS servers from the DHCP-provided list, since the local server forwards external queries anyway. Then flush the cache with `sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder`.
key_points: nslookup/dig bypass the system resolver and use /etc/resolv.conf directly, so they succeed while ssh and other apps fail
Snow Leopard apps resolve through mDNSResponder, which may reorder the DNS servers it queries
Querying the ISP DNS servers, which don't know internal names, causes the failure
Fix: list only the internal DNS server(s), removing the ISP servers from DHCP if necessary, and flush the cache with killall -HUP mDNSResponder

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer, including mDNSResponder using a different resolver path/order than nslookup/dig and the recommendation to remove ISP DNS servers and flush mDNSResponder. However, the scenario explicitly includes the crucial cause details: DHCP supplies both internal and ISP DNS servers, internal names are only on the internal server, split DNS is used, and failures are intermittent in other apps. That strongly hints at the root cause, so no_leak is false. The scenario is clearly solvable, and the accepted answer identifies one primary cause.

item.scenario:
Fresh MariaDB install on an Ubuntu 19.10 workstation using `sudo apt install mariadb-server mariadb-client`. Running `sudo systemctl start mariadb.service` hangs the shell indefinitely and has to be interrupted with Ctrl+C. Other units start normally with systemctl.

Status after about 5 minutes:
```
mariadb.service - MariaDB 10.3.22 database server
 Loaded: loaded (/lib/systemd/system/mariadb.service; enabled; vendor preset: enabled)
 Drop-In: /etc/systemd/system/mariadb.service.d
  └─migrated-from-my.cnf-settings.conf
 Active: activating (start) since Mon 2020-04-20 08:44:57 IST; 5min ago
 Process: 10705 ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/install -m 755 -o mysql -g root -d /var/run/mysqld (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS)
 Process: 10707 ExecStartPre=/bin/sh -c systemctl unset-environment _WSREP_START_POSITION (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS)
 Process: 10711 ExecStartPre=... galera_recovery ...
 Main PID: 10759 (mysqld)
 Tasks: 15  Memory: 64.6M
```
The journal shows only:
```
mysqld[10759]: [Note] /usr/sbin/mysqld (mysqld 10.3.22-MariaDB-0ubuntu0.19.10.1) starting as process 10759 ...
```
mysqld stays running, but the unit never leaves the activating state. Nothing else is logged.
item.root_cause: MySQL was installed on the machine earlier. It left an AppArmor profile for /usr/sbin/mysqld that the MariaDB package did not remove. That stale profile confines MariaDB's mysqld, so startup never completes and the unit stays in activating. This is a known Ubuntu packaging bug.
item.fix: Stop mariadb. Overwrite /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.mysqld with an empty profile (`/usr/sbin/mysqld { }`) and unload it with `apparmor_parser -v -R`. Symlink the profile into /etc/apparmor.d/disable/ so it does not return after a reboot, then start mariadb again.
key_points: A previous MySQL installation left an AppArmor profile for /usr/sbin/mysqld
The MariaDB package fails to remove or replace that profile, which is a known bug
The profile must be unloaded with apparmor_parser -R
The profile must be disabled via a symlink in /etc/apparmor.d/disable, otherwise it comes back after reboot

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: per-server ssl_protocols ineffective with SNI-based virtual hosts sharing an IP; protocol negotiated before SNI selects the vhost.
item.scenario: We run nginx 1.8.0 on Debian (OpenSSL 1.0.1f) as a TLS-terminating reverse proxy for several sites on the same box. One of those sites has to pass PCI DSS, and the latest Trustwave scan failed it because TLS 1.0 is still accepted. The http block in nginx.conf has `ssl_protocols TLSv1 TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2;`. The server block for the PCI site sets `ssl_protocols TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2;`. We have also tried moving the SSL directives out of the http block into each SSL server block and changing the cipher list. After every change and reload, `openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -tls1` still completes a TLS 1.0 handshake. SSL Labs rates the site A but lists TLS 1.0 as enabled. The other SSL settings appear correct. Only the protocol restriction for this one site seems to have no effect.
item.root_cause: The site shares an IP:port with other virtual hosts, and nginx selects the server block from SNI. The TLS protocol version is negotiated before SNI chooses that server block, so the per-server ssl_protocols cannot take effect. The protocols of the default/first server on that listener are used instead.
item.fix: Give the PCI site its own dedicated IP address with no other virtual hosts on it. nginx can then apply that server's ssl_protocols (TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2) based on the IP and refuse TLS 1.0.
key_points: Multiple SNI-based virtual hosts share the same IP:443
Protocol version is negotiated before the SNI-selected server block applies
The per-server ssl_protocols is effectively ignored
Fix by binding the site to a dedicated IP so its settings apply at connection time

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: TLS protocol negotiation occurs before SNI-based virtual host selection, so per-vhost protocol settings cannot disable TLS 1.0 unless the site is isolated by IP. The scenario includes the relevant symptoms and multi-site nginx setup without explicitly naming SNI or the root cause.

item.scenario:
While chasing slow performance on our office network, I ran traceroute against several large public sites. Most destinations complete. yahoo.com, amazon.com and ebay.com never do, and the result repeats every time.

Example against ebay.com, run with the default traceroute and no options:
```
traceroute: Warning: ebay.com has multiple addresses; using 66.135.205.13
traceroute to ebay.com (66.135.205.13), 64 hops max, 52 byte packets

 2 mo-69-34-118-1.sta.embarqhsd.net  9.943 ms ...
 ...

 9 chp-brdr-03.inet.qwest.net  26.315 ms ...
10 dvr-edge-13.inet.qwest.net  51.270 ms 51.355 ms 51.134 ms

...

```
Latency looks normal through hop 10. After that every probe times out until I cancel. Is something on our side breaking these traces, and does it relate to our performance problem?
item.root_cause: The destination networks use firewalls that filter the traffic default traceroute relies on: UDP probes to unlikely high ports, and/or the ICMP replies. Hops past their edge therefore never answer. This reflects filtering on the target networks, not a fault in the operator's network.
item.fix: Use a traceroute method that firewalls are likely to allow. `traceroute -I` sends ICMP echo probes and `traceroute -T` sends TCP SYN probes; either should get further or complete (yahoo.com completes this way).
key_points: Default traceroute probes (UDP to high ports, relying on ICMP responses) are filtered by firewalls on the destination networks

Using ICMP echo (-I) or TCP SYN (-T) probe methods works around the filtering

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: the tar run actually succeeds; the warnings come from Unix domain socket files that tar cannot archive. Excluding the sockets via -X restores a meaningful exit code.
item.scenario:
I'm trying to take a full-system backup of a CentOS server with GNU tar:

 tar cvpzf /TEMP_BACKUPS/backup.tgz --exclude=/proc --exclude=/lost+found --exclude=/tmp --exclude=/TEMP_BACKUPS --exclude=/mnt --exclude=/sys / > /TEMP_BACKUPS/mylog.txt

The file listing goes to mylog.txt, but stderr shows a long list of messages, and tar exits non-zero. I ran it twice and got the same result. Excerpt:

 tar: Removing leading `/' from member names
 tar: /dev/log: socket ignored
 tar: /selinux/policy: Cannot open: Invalid argument
 tar: /var/spool/postfix/public/flush: socket ignored
 tar: /var/spool/postfix/private/smtp: socket ignored
 tar: /var/lib/mysql/mysql.sock: socket ignored
 tar: /var/www/html/run/wsgi.1458.0.1.sock: socket ignored
 tar: /var/run/dbus/system_bus_socket: socket ignored
 tar: /var/run/nscd/socket: socket ignored
 tar: Exiting with failure status due to previous errors

There are dozens more of the same kind under /var/spool/postfix and /var/run. Is the backup broken? What do I need to change so the full backup completes cleanly and I can rely on tar's exit status to tell whether it worked?
item.root_cause: The archive is actually being created. tar cannot store Unix domain socket files, so it reports each one as 'socket ignored'. Those diagnostics make tar exit with a failure status even though the rest of the filesystem was archived.
item.fix: Build a list of socket files with `find / -type s -print > /tmp/sockets-to-exclude` and pass it to tar with `-X /tmp/sockets-to-exclude`. tar then skips them without complaint, and its exit code becomes a useful success indicator. The other --exclude entries can also go into an exclude file used with -X/--exclude-from.
key_points: The tar backup itself completed; the messages are warnings about socket files
tar cannot archive Unix domain sockets and reports 'socket ignored'
These warnings cause tar to exit with a non-zero failure status
Exclude sockets, e.g. via find / -type s into an exclude list used with -X, to get a clean exit code

The scenario includes enough evidence to solve it, and the accepted answer focuses on one primary cause.

item.scenario:
A user on an Ubuntu laptop routinely SSHes to a remote server (example.org, port 22). On one specific Wi-Fi access point, every connection attempt aborts with 'WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!'. The client reports a different ED25519 fingerprint and an offending key in ~/.ssh/known_hosts line 3, then 'Host key verification failed.'

Switching to another network, such as a phone hotspot, makes the connection work normally with the original key. The problem persists across OS reinstalls. The problem network belongs to an academic institution and appears heavily restricted; for example, torrent traffic is blocked.

A Wireshark capture on the problem network shows:
- The DNS query to 8.8.8.8 for example.org returns the same IP as on other networks.
- The SSH key exchange looks normal.
- The host key in the 'ECDH Key Exchange Reply' has a different fingerprint from the one received on other networks.

The server's configuration is believed to be unchanged. The user wants to know what is happening and whether SSH can be used safely on this network.
item.root_cause: Something on that access point's network path is intercepting the SSH connection, acting as a man-in-the-middle. It presents its own host key instead of the real server's. The server's host keys have not actually changed.
item.fix: Do not accept the new key. Treat the connection through that AP as compromised until the cause is explained. Contact the AP or network administrator to report the interception and track it down; until then, avoid using SSH over that network.
key_points: The host key mismatch occurs only on one network while DNS/IP are the same, so the server's key did not change
A device on that network path is intercepting the SSH session (MITM) and presenting a different host key
Do not remove or override the known_hosts entry; treat the connection as compromised
Raise the issue with the access point's or institution's network administrator

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: nginx is configured to pass PHP to a FastCGI backend at 127.0.0.1:9000, but nothing is listening there, so the connection is refused.
item.scenario:
Users get HTTP 502 Bad Gateway when requesting a PHP page under a subdirectory (http://domain.com/dev/index.php). Static content on the same nginx server appears to work. This is the first time the operator has seen this error on the box.

The nginx error log has this entry for each failed request:

2011/09/30 23:47:54 [error] 31160#0: *35 connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream, client: xx.xx.xx.xx, server: domain.com, request: "GET /dev/ HTTP/1.1", upstream: "fastcgi://127.0.0.1:9000", host: "domain.com"

nginx.conf is a stock Debian/Ubuntu-style config: user www-data, 4 worker processes, 768 worker_connections, sendfile and gzip on, logging to /var/log/nginx/, and includes for conf.d/*.conf and sites-enabled/*. A site config sends .php requests to FastCGI at 127.0.0.1:9000. Nothing has been changed yet.
item.root_cause: No FastCGI/PHP backend (php-fpm) is running and listening on 127.0.0.1:9000. nginx tries to hand the PHP request to that upstream, the TCP connection is refused, and nginx returns 502.
item.fix: Install and start php-fpm and configure it to listen on 127.0.0.1:9000. Make sure nginx has a `location ~ \.php$` block with `fastcgi_pass 127.0.0.1:9000;`, then reload nginx.
key_points: Error 111 Connection refused means nothing is listening on the upstream address 127.0.0.1:9000
The upstream is a FastCGI PHP backend (php-fpm) that is not running or not configured
nginx itself is fine; the 502 comes from the missing backend
Starting php-fpm on port 9000 and pointing fastcgi_pass at it resolves the error

audit.notes: The accepted answer directly says the backend for nginx has not been started/configured and to start php-fpm with fastcgi_pass to 127.0.0.1:9000. The scenario includes the key log evidence without explicitly stating php-fpm is down. An engineer could reasonably infer the refused FastCGI connection means no backend is listening. item.reason: Single identifiable root cause: the existence of /etc/ssh/sshrc prevents sshd from running xauth, so the forwarded display's cookie is never added on the server. The scenario can be written to include the ssh -vvv log showing the wrong-authentication rejection without naming the cause.
item.scenario:
Remote X apps fail over SSH from my work desktop to my home box (KDE 4.6.5, Qt 4.7.4). The SSH login itself works, but no X11 application will display.

Home sshd_config:
- X11Forwarding yes
- X11DisplayOffset 10
- X11UseLocalhost yes

Work-side configuration:
- ssh_config sets ForwardX11 yes and ForwardX11Trusted yes.
- ~/.ssh/config for host 'home' also sets ForwardX11 yes.

What I've tried:
- xhost +home, then ssh -X and ssh -Y, by both hostname and IP.
- Checked ~/.Xauthority on both machines: each exists, mode 600, owned by me.
- Port 22 is allowed in iptables at home.

After login, DISPLAY is localhost:10.0. Running kate prints "X11 connection rejected because of wrong authentication." about 8 times, then "kate: cannot connect to X server localhost:10.0".

With -vvv the client shows:
- "x11_get_proto: /usr/bin/xauth list :0"
- "Requesting X11 forwarding with authentication spoofing"
- When kate starts: "client_request_x11: request from 127.0.0.1 ...", "confirm x11", "X11 connection uses different authentication protocol.", then the rejection and the channel closing.
item.root_cause: The home server has an /etc/ssh/sshrc file. When ~/.ssh/rc or /etc/ssh/sshrc exists, sshd runs it instead of running xauth itself. Because that file did not add the forwarded X11 cookie, the display localhost:10 had no matching xauth entry on the server, and connections were rejected with wrong authentication.
item.fix: Add the xauth handling snippet from the sshd man page to /etc/ssh/sshrc (or ~/.ssh/rc) on the server. It reads the proto and cookie from stdin and pipes 'add unix:<display> $proto $cookie' (or 'add $DISPLAY ...' when X11UseLocalhost=no) to 'xauth -q -'.

An existing /etc/ssh/sshrc on the server meant the X11 cookie for the forwarded display was never added
Server-side xauth lacks the proper cookie, so connections are rejected with wrong authentication
Fix: make the rc file read proto/cookie and call xauth add for the display

item.scenario:
Test box running CentOS 6.2 with PostgreSQL 9.1 from the official RPM repo. phpPgAdmin 5.0.4 was unpacked by hand under Apache's docroot.

Changes made so far:
- Every METHOD in pg_hba.conf set to md5.
- A password set on the postgres role.
- A new role 'webuser' created with a password and nothing else.
- In phpPgAdmin's config.inc.php, $conf['servers'][0]['host'] changed from '' to '127.0.0.1' (localhost also tried).
- $conf['extra_login_security'] set to false.

Every login attempt through the phpPgAdmin web UI returns a plain "Login failed". This includes the exact same credentials that work fine with psql from a shell on the box. The phpPgAdmin FAQ troubleshooting steps for login problems were followed without success. A forum post suggesting tcpip_socket=true in postgresql.conf was tried, and PostgreSQL refused to start until it was removed. Apart from the md5 auth changes, postgresql.conf and the OS are at their defaults. The operator is new to PostgreSQL and needs the web UI to log in.
item.root_cause: The PHP application running under Apache could not open a TCP connection to PostgreSQL. On CentOS, SELinux blocks httpd from making network connections to databases by default (httpd_can_network_connect_db is off). PostgreSQL may also not have been listening on TCP (listen_addresses). psql worked because it ran outside Apache's SELinux context.
item.fix: Allow Apache to connect to databases with `setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db 1`. Make sure PostgreSQL accepts TCP connections by setting listen_addresses (e.g. '*' or 'localhost') in postgresql.conf, then restart PostgreSQL. Do not use the obsolete tcpip_socket option, which breaks startup on 9.1.
key_points: The failure is in the network/TCP path from Apache/PHP to PostgreSQL, not the credentials themselves
SELinux on CentOS blocks httpd database network connections by default; enable the httpd_can_network_connect_db boolean
PostgreSQL must be listening on TCP via listen_addresses in postgresql.conf (tcpip_socket is obsolete in 9.1)
item.technology: PostgreSQL 9.1 / phpPgAdmin / Apache / SELinux on CentOS 6

audit.notes: The root cause/fix match the accepted answer: Apache/PHP could not connect over TCP due to SELinux and possibly PostgreSQL listen settings, fixed with setsebool and listen_addresses. However the scenario includes the tcpip_socket detail from the answer, which strongly hints at the TCP/IP root cause. The reference is also framed as a combination/possible pair of causes rather than a single clean cause.

item.reason: A clear diagnosis case. The client refuses the connection because the stored host key for the server no longer matches the key the server presents. The accepted answer gives a probable cause and a targeted fix.
item.scenario:
An operator connects to a Linux server (host1) as root over SSH and gets a large warning banner every time. It says the remote host identification has changed and that a man-in-the-middle attack is possible. It shows the RSA fingerprint the server is now sending (93:a2:1b:1c:5f:3e:68:47:bf:79:56:52:f0:ec:03:6b). It points to an offending key at /home/emerson/.ssh/known_hosts:377, says strict checking is requested, and ends with 'Host key verification failed.'

The operator says that in some attempts a shell prompt (host1:~/.ssh #) appears for a few seconds. The session then drops with 'Read from remote host host1: Connection reset by peer' and 'Connection to host1 closed.'

The operator wants to know what is happening. They also want to know whether they should just turn off strict host key checking or wipe their known_hosts file so they can work normally again.
item.root_cause: The RSA host key presented by host1 no longer matches the one cached in the client's ~/.ssh/known_hosts at line 377. This is most likely because an SSH upgrade or reinstall on the server regenerated its host keys, leaving a stale entry on the client. The client's strict host key checking therefore rejects the connection.
item.fix: First confirm out-of-band that host1 really is the intended machine and that the new fingerprint is legitimate. Then remove only the stale entry, either with `sed -i 377d ~/.ssh/known_hosts` or with `ssh-keygen -R host1` (or the server's IP), and reconnect to accept the new key. Do not delete the whole known_hosts file or disable strict checking.
key_points: The server's host key differs from the cached entry in ~/.ssh/known_hosts (line 377)
The likely reason is that the server's host keys were regenerated, e.g. by an SSH upgrade
Verify the server's identity before trusting the new key, since this warning protects against man-in-the-middle attacks
Remove only the specific offending entry (sed line 377 or ssh-keygen -R), not the whole known_hosts file and not strict checking

audit.notes: The accepted answer supports the host-key mismatch/stale known_hosts entry and the specific-line removal fixes, with verification first. The scenario itself directly includes the SSH warning, offending known_hosts line, and strict checking failure, so it strongly reveals the root cause. The evidence is sufficient to solve, and the item centers on one primary cause: cached host key mismatch.

item.reason: Clear single root cause (stale known_hosts entry for a reused Elastic IP) with concrete evidence in the debug output.
item.scenario: We run an Ubuntu EC2 instance in the Singapore region with a Rails app deployed on it. The app serves traffic fine, but SSH logins to the box keep failing every time we try. The instance has an Elastic IP (46.137.253.231) attached, and the console isn't showing a public DNS name for it. Client is OpenSSH_5.8p1 (Ubuntu); server reports OpenSSH_5.5p1 Debian-4ubuntu6. Running ssh -v with our st.pem key shows the TCP connection succeeds, protocol 2.0 is negotiated, and KEX completes up to SSH2_MSG_KEX_DH_GEX_REPLY. Then the client prints a large banner warning that the remote host identification has changed and that a man-in-the-middle is possible. It also says: 'Offending RSA key in /home/ubuntu/.ssh/known_hosts:1', 'RSA host key for 46.137.253.231 has changed and you have requested strict checking.' The final line is 'Host key verification failed.' Authentication never begins. Retrying gives the same result every time.
item.root_cause: The SSH client's known_hosts file still holds a host key fingerprint stored for 46.137.253.231 from an earlier EC2 instance that used the same IP. The new instance now on that Elastic IP presents a different host key, so strict host key checking rejects it.
item.fix: Remove the stale entry with `ssh-keygen -f ~/.ssh/known_hosts -R 46.137.253.231`, or delete line 1 of known_hosts by hand. Also remove any extra lines stored for the hostname or IPv6 address, then reconnect and accept the new host key. Only do this after confirming the key change is expected.
key_points: known_hosts stores IP-to-host-key fingerprint pairs
The IP/Elastic IP was reused by a different EC2 instance with a different host key
The stale entry at known_hosts line 1 must be removed (ssh-keygen -R or manual edit)
Verify the key change is expected before removing, since it could otherwise indicate MITM

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer. The scenario includes the key SSH warning and known_hosts line, which strongly points to the known_hosts host-key mismatch, so no_leak is false. It is solvable from the provided evidence, and the accepted answer identifies one primary cause.

item.reason: The accepted answer names two concrete causes. First, wg setconf does not accept wg-quick fields such as Address. Second, IP forwarding was written to sysctl.conf but never applied to the running kernel, so peers could not route through the server.
item.scenario:
I'm building a WireGuard VPN on an Ubuntu 18.04.4 server (kernel 4.15.0-20, wireguard-tools v1.0.20200206). The goal is for clients to reach each other and the Internet through the tunnel. The client is a Mac using the WireGuard GUI.

Server wg0.conf has an [Interface] section with Address=10.0.0.1/24, ListenPort 5555 and a private key, plus one [Peer] with AllowedIPs=0.0.0.0/0. Loading it with `wg setconf wg0 /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf` fails with:

Line unrecognized: `Address=10.0.0.1/24'
Configuration parsing error

I commented out that line and created the interface by hand with `ip link add dev wg0 type wireguard`, `ip address add dev wg0 10.0.0.1/24` and `ip link set up dev wg0`. `wg` now shows a recent handshake and some bytes transferred.

From the Mac I can ping 10.0.0.1 and reach nginx on the private IP. With client AllowedIPs=0.0.0.0/0, ::/0 I lose all Internet access and can't even ping the server's public IP. Two clients also can't reach each other.

There is no iptables or firewall on the server. I added net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 to /etc/sysctl.conf and restarted systemd-networkd.
item.root_cause: There are two problems. The plain `wg setconf` tool does not understand wg-quick-only fields such as Address, so the config was being loaded with the wrong tool. Separately, the forwarding settings added to /etc/sysctl.conf were never applied to the running kernel, so the server did not forward traffic between peers or out to the Internet.
item.fix: Bring the interface up with wg-quick (for example through the systemd wg-quick@wg0 service) instead of `wg setconf`. Apply the forwarding settings with `sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.conf`. Add PostUp/PostDown rules that accept FORWARD traffic on wg0 and MASQUERADE out of eth0 so clients can reach the Internet.
key_points: wg setconf does not accept wg-quick fields like Address; use wg-quick
Editing /etc/sysctl.conf alone did not enable forwarding; it must be applied with sysctl -p
Restarting systemd-networkd or running daemon-reload does not apply the sysctl settings
Clients need forwarding plus NAT (MASQUERADE) on the server to reach the Internet and each other

audit.notes: The item matches the accepted answer's two stated issues: using wg setconf for wg-quick-style fields like Address, and sysctl.conf forwarding settings not being applied with sysctl -p. The PostUp/PostDown NAT/FORWARD rules are present in the accepted configuration, though the answer qualifies them as needed only with ufw. The scenario includes the relevant evidence without explicitly naming the causes. However, the reference root cause is explicitly two problems, so it is not a single primary cause.

item.reason: The thread has one clear root cause: the key directive points at the CSR file. The config fragment and log errors give enough evidence to diagnose it.
item.scenario:
We're enabling HTTPS on an Ubuntu 14.04 box running Apache with mod_ssl. In default-ssl.conf we set:

SSLCertificateFile /etc/apache2/ssl/domain.crt
SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/apache2/ssl/domain.csr

After enabling the site and restarting Apache, the service will not start. /var/log/apache2/error.log shows:

[ssl:error] AH02203: Init: Private key not found
[ssl:error] SSL Library Error: error:0D0680A8:asn1 encoding routines:ASN1_CHECK_TLEN:wrong tag
[ssl:error] SSL Library Error: error:0D08303A:asn1 encoding routines:ASN1_TEMPLATE_NOEXP_D2I:nested asn1 error
[ssl:error] SSL Library Error: error:04093004:rsa routines:OLD_RSA_PRIV_DECODE:RSA lib
[ssl:error] SSL Library Error: error:0D07803A:asn1 encoding routines:ASN1_ITEM_EX_D2I:nested asn1 error
[ssl:emerg] AH02311: Fatal error initialising mod_ssl, exiting.

The files exist under /etc/apache2/ssl and are readable. Why won't mod_ssl initialise?
item.root_cause: SSLCertificateKeyFile points at the certificate signing request (domain.csr), not at the private key. mod_ssl fails to parse the CSR as an RSA private key, which produces the ASN.1 'wrong tag' errors and 'Private key not found'.
item.fix: Point SSLCertificateKeyFile at the actual private key file, the one beginning with 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY' that was generated with the CSR. If that key has been lost, generate a new private key and a new CSR, and have the CA sign the certificate again.
key_points: SSLCertificateKeyFile is set to the .csr file, not to a private key
A CSR is only used to request a certificate signature; it is not a private key
The correct file is the private key generated alongside the CSR ('BEGIN PRIVATE KEY')
If the key is lost, generate a new key and CSR and have the certificate reissued

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: Apache was configured to use the CSR as the private key, and the fix is to point SSLCertificateKeyFile to the actual private key or regenerate key/CSR if lost. The scenario is solvable because it includes the relevant Apache SSL config and errors. However, it strongly hints at the root cause by explicitly showing SSLCertificateKeyFile set to a .csr file alongside 'Private key not found'. The reference has one primary cause.

item.reason: Clear single root cause (Synology-patched sshd hard-codes allowed shells for non-root/admin users) with evidence in the question sufficient to reason toward it.
item.scenario: Synology DS212+ (ARM, DSM 4.1) NAS. I installed bash and set it as the login shell for several accounts. root, with /bin/bash in /etc/passwd, logs in over SSH with no trouble. A regular account (joeuser, uid 1029, shell /bin/bash) authenticates fine. The 'Last login' banner prints, then the session immediately shows 'Permission denied, please try again.' and the connection closes. If I switch joeuser's shell back to /bin/sh, SSH login works. With /bin/bash the same user can log in on the serial console, and 'su - joeuser' as root also works, so the bash binary itself is fine. As a test I changed joeuser's uid to 0, and SSH still failed. sshd_config has UsePAM yes, PermitRootLogin yes, ChrootDirectory none, and an internal-sftp subsystem, with nothing unusual. I ran the vendor daemon in debug mode (/usr/syno/sbin/sshd -d, OpenSSH_5.8p1-hpn13v11) with LogLevel DEBUG. Nothing in the output explains the rejection.
item.root_cause: Synology's sshd is a vendor-modified OpenSSH build. In do_child() (session.c) it calls a hard-coded IsAllowShell() check. That check grants shell sessions only to the usernames root or admin, or to users whose passwd shell is exactly /bin/sh or /bin/ash. Any other user/shell combination gets 'Permission denied, please try again.' and the process exits, whatever the uid.
item.fix: Rebuild Synology's OpenSSH 5.8p1 source (from their GPL release) with the IsAllowShell() check removed. Cross-compile it for the NAS CPU (Marvell Kirkwood) and replace the vendor sshd binary. Alternatively, keep users on /bin/sh or /bin/ash.
key_points: Synology ships a customized OpenSSH sshd, not stock OpenSSH
A hard-coded check (IsAllowShell) in session.c allows only /bin/sh or /bin/ash for users other than root/admin
The check goes by username and shell string, not uid, which is why uid=0 didn't help
Fix is to recompile sshd without that check (or use an allowed shell)

audit.notes: The item accurately reflects the accepted answer: Synology's customized sshd hard-codes allowed shells for non-root/admin users, and the fix is to remove that check/rebuild or use /bin/sh or /bin/ash. The scenario includes the original diagnostic evidence without explicitly revealing the IsAllowShell root cause. The cause is singular and primary.

item.reason: The error and the context (an NFS server crash followed by a failure to take a lock) point to one identifiable cause: the NFS lock daemon is not running. The answer lists other possibilities, but it settles on lockd once the crash is known.
item.scenario:
Developers report that commits to our Subversion server have started failing. The repository lives on an NFS share mounted on the SVN host at /svn/repo. Every commit attempt aborts with:

```
svn: Can't get exclusive lock on file '/svn/repo/db/transactions/7802-2.txn/rev-lock': No locks available
```

Commits worked fine until recently. Nobody has upgraded or changed software on the SVN host or the storage side. The one notable event is that the NFS file server crashed and was brought back up earlier today. Since then, every commit has hit this error. Reads and checkouts appear unaffected. We're unsure whether the crash left something 'corrupted' in the repository. We need to know why exclusive file locks can't be obtained on the share.
item.root_cause: After the NFS server crashed and came back up, its lock daemon (lockd) was not running. Without lockd, NFS file-locking requests fail, so SVN cannot take an exclusive lock on the rev-lock file and gets ENOLCK ('No locks available').
item.fix: Start the NFS lock daemon (lockd, and the related lock/status services) on the NFS server. Configure it to start automatically whenever the NFS server reboots.
key_points: 'No locks available' (ENOLCK) on an NFS mount points to NFS file locking failing, not to repository corruption
The NFS lock daemon (lockd) is not running on the NFS server after the crash and reboot
lockd must be started and enabled to launch at NFS server boot
item.technology: NFS / Linux file locking (lockd) with Subversion

audit.notes: The accepted answer lists multiple possibilities, though it later says the crash/reboot makes lockd not running the likely cause. The item’s root cause and fix are faithful to that update, and the scenario includes the necessary evidence without explicitly naming lockd.

reason: The accepted answer does not identify one definite root cause. It suggests several possibilities: messages going to a different file, being filtered by syslog.conf, or needing an sshd restart. It also only points to man pages, and the question has no evidence that would let someone settle on one cause.

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: shell redirection runs with the calling user's privileges, not sudo's.
item.scenario:
I'm automating setup of an AWS EC2 Ubuntu instance as part of a build pipeline and need to enable IPv4 forwarding non-interactively. Manual edits aren't an option. The build step runs this:

```
sudo echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1" >> /etc/sysctl.conf
```

It fails with:

```
Permission denied
```

This is confusing because sudo has worked for every other privileged command in the same script, such as package installs and service restarts. In an interactive SSH session, if I run `sudo su` first and then the same echo/append line, it works and the line ends up in /etc/sysctl.conf. I need a way to make this work from the script without dropping into an interactive root shell or editing the file by hand.
item.root_cause: The `>>` redirection is performed by the calling, unprivileged shell before sudo runs. Only `echo` gets elevated, so the shell opening /etc/sysctl.conf for append is denied.
item.fix: Run the whole command, including the redirection, under root. For example: `sudo /bin/su -c "echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1' >> /etc/sysctl.conf"`. Alternatively, copy the file to /tmp, append there, and `sudo cp` it back to /etc.
key_points: Redirection (>, >>, <) is handled by the calling shell, not the command run via sudo
sudo only elevates the echo process, not the file open for append
The fix is to run the redirection inside a root shell (sudo su -c / sh -c) or write elsewhere and sudo cp the file back

audit.notes: The item accurately reflects the accepted answer: sudo elevates echo but not the shell redirection, and the suggested fixes match. The scenario includes the relevant command and symptoms without explicitly explaining the redirection issue. An experienced engineer could solve it from the given evidence, and the reference has one primary cause.

item.reason: The accepted answer gives an identifiable cause: a catch-all routing setting collects mail for random addresses, and the X-Google-DKIM-Signature header is misread. The scenario can carry the evidence without revealing the cause.
item.scenario:
Our small company domain is hosted on Google Apps, and every user sends through the Gmail web interface. For the past few weeks our inbox has been filling with delivery-failure notices. Each one concerns mail that appears to come from a random, nonexistent mailbox on our domain, e.g. onSecNtV1@ourdomain.com, sent to strangers. The admin console shows no unusual account activity and no unknown users. I looked for a setting to block sending from unregistered addresses and found none.

Sample bounce: "Google tried to deliver your message, but it was rejected by the server for the recipient domain 174.133.125.2 ... 553 sorry, that domain isn't in my list of allowed rcpthosts (#5.7.1)". The quoted original contains:
- an X-Google-DKIM-Signature with d=google.com, s=20120113
- Return-Path <onSecNtV1@ourdomain.com>
- Received: from [117.201.44.87] ([117.201.34.157]) by mx.google.com
- Received-SPF: neutral (117.201.34.157 is neither permitted nor denied by best guess record for domain ...)
- Subject "I will be excited if you are my Valetine"

The DKIM header and the "Google tried to deliver" wording make me worry the spam originates from our own trusted clients. Where is the leak?
item.root_cause: The Google Apps domain has a catch-all address enabled. All mail addressed to any random, nonexistent username at the domain, including spam and bounce backscatter for spoofed senders, is accepted and delivered to the admin's mailbox. The X-Google-DKIM-Signature header is a Gmail-internal header, not a DKIM signature for the customer's domain, so it does not show the mail came from the user's accounts.
item.fix: Disable the catch-all address setting in the Google Apps admin console so mail for nonexistent users is rejected. Ignore the X-Google-DKIM-Signature header. If real domain authentication is wanted, set up DKIM signing for the domain in Google Apps.
key_points: A catch-all address is enabled, so mail to any random username at the domain is delivered to a real mailbox
The bounces for random usernames are spoofed or backscatter traffic, not proof that an account was compromised
X-Google-DKIM-Signature (d=google.com) is Gmail-specific and is not a DKIM signature for the user's domain
The domain has no real DKIM for its own name and no SPF record (SPF result is 'neutral', based on a best guess); real domain DKIM must be configured separately
item.technology: Google Apps (G Suite) email / DKIM / SPF

audit.notes: The item matches the accepted answer: catch-all enabled causes receipt of random-address bounces, and X-Google-DKIM-Signature is not domain DKIM. The scenario includes the necessary evidence without naming catch-all. The accepted answer gives one primary cause, with DKIM clarification as supporting explanation.

item.reason: Clear diagnosis: posixGroup/posixAccount/shadowAccount object classes are undefined because the nis schema isn't loaded.
item.scenario:
Setting up a first test OpenLDAP server on Ubuntu, following the distro's basic setup guide. I wrote an LDIF that creates ou=People and ou=Groups (organizationalUnit), a group cn=engineers with objectClass posixGroup and gidNumber 5000, and a user uid=john with objectClasses inetOrgPerson, posixAccount and shadowAccount (uidNumber 10000, gidNumber 5000, loginShell, homeDirectory, gecos, userPassword).

Loaded it with:
  ldapadd -x -D cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com -W -f add_content.ldif

The two OUs seem fine, but the group and user entries fail:
  adding new entry "cn=engineers,ou=Groups,dc=my-domain,dc=com"
  ldap_add: Invalid syntax (21)
    additional info: objectClass: value #0 invalid per syntax
  adding new entry "uid=john,ou=People,dc=my-domain,dc=com"
  ldap_add: Invalid syntax (21)
    additional info: objectClass: value #0 invalid per syntax

Server is configured through a slapd.conf file. Searching the error message turned up nothing useful. Why are these entries rejected?
item.root_cause: The nis schema, which defines the posixGroup, posixAccount and shadowAccount object classes, isn't loaded in slapd. The server treats those objectClass values as unknown and rejects them as invalid syntax.
item.fix: With slapd.conf, add an include line for nis.schema (e.g. include /usr/local/etc/openldap/schema/nis.schema, adjusting the path) and restart slapd. With cn=config, load nis.ldif instead, e.g. ldapadd -Y EXTERNAL -H ldapi:// -f .../nis.ldif. No restart is needed in that case.
key_points: posixGroup/posixAccount/shadowAccount come from the nis schema
nis schema is not loaded in the server
Fix by including nis.schema in slapd.conf and restarting slapd (or ldapadd nis.ldif under cn=config)

audit.notes: The item matches the accepted answer: the missing nis schema is the primary cause, and the slapd.conf/cn=config fixes are accurately represented. The scenario includes the relevant failing objectClasses and error output without explicitly naming the missing schema. It provides enough evidence for an experienced OpenLDAP user to infer the missing schema issue, and the accepted answer gives a single primary cause.

item.reason: Clear single root cause: the home directory permissions (700) block nginx from traversing into the web root.
item.scenario:
Local Ubuntu 12.04 box running nginx 1.1.19. nginx.conf is stock apart from the user directive, now `user nginx www-data;`. A test vhost serves static files with `root /home;`, `index index.html`, `server_name localhost`, and `try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html`.

A page at /home/index.html loads fine at http://localhost/. I changed root to /home/ubuntu, moved the file to /home/ubuntu/index.html, recreated the sites-enabled symlink, and stopped and started nginx. Now every request returns 403 Forbidden.

The file itself shows `-rw-r--r-- 1 nginx www-data 183 ... index.html`. Running chmod 777 on it made no difference. `/etc/init.d/nginx configtest` reports no errors, and the symlink is correct.

The same behaviour appears on an EC2 Ubuntu 12.04 instance. I wondered whether home-directory encryption is involved, but I can't see why content under the user's home folder can't be served when the same file one level up works.
item.root_cause: The user's home directory /home/ubuntu has default permissions 700 on Ubuntu 12.04, so the nginx worker user has no execute (traverse) permission on that parent directory. It therefore cannot reach the file, whatever the file's own permissions are.
item.fix: Give others execute permission on the home directory with `chmod 701 /home/ubuntu` (or 755). Make sure every directory on the path to the web root is executable by the nginx user/group, and every served file is readable by it.
key_points: Ubuntu home directories default to mode 700
nginx needs execute permission on every parent directory along the path, not just read on the file
Changing the file's own permissions (even 777) does not help when a parent directory blocks traversal
Fix: chmod 701 or 755 on the home directory

audit.notes: The root cause and fix match the accepted answer: nginx can read the file but cannot traverse the user's home directory because of default 700 permissions; chmod 701/755 and ensuring directory execute/file read permissions fixes it. The scenario includes the relevant evidence without explicitly stating the directory permission issue. The accepted answer identifies one primary cause.
